In this work, we analyze notions that are closely related to this property. To understand which [MATH]-flats of [MATH] remain flats under [MATH], we study the [MATH]-breaking. The function [MATH] has been studied in the past in this context---we extend this study to general mappings and characterize the 2-breaking of APN functions. Recently, two generalizations of the APN property have been introduced: [MATH]-strongly non-normality and [MATH]-th-order sum-freedom. Sum-freedom generalizes the non-vanishing property of APN functions to higher dimensional flats. We provide in-depth observations of the relations between the breaking property, strongly non-normality and sum-freedom. We show that a 3rd-order sum-free APN function must be 3-breaking. We introduce a fourth concept called [MATH]-strongly breaking, which implies the breaking property. We derive several structural results for both notions and give a characterization of a subclass of APN functions in terms of the 2-strongly breaking property. We propose a different perspective of the non-vanishing property via a natural character transformation, which is closely related to the sum-of-square indicator of the components of [MATH]. We derive a precise value for the total sum of the sum-of-square indicators of [MATH]. With this approach, we provide a simple answer to Open Problem 4 in IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 52(9): 4160-4170, 2006. Moreover, it allows us to explore balancedness properties of polynomials, one of which characterizes component-wise APNness, for odd [MATH], and provides a natural extension to any dimension. We show that Dillon's APN permutation and the Gold functions satisfy a related property, termed [MATH]-balanced, which is presented under our framework.
tldr: The paper analyzes relationships among several notions related to APN mappings, including breaking properties, strong non-normality, sum-freedom, and a character-transform perspective linked to the sum-of-square indicator.
motivation: APN mappings are central in cryptography and coding theory, and several generalized notions have recently been introduced, motivating a unified structural study and the resolution of an open problem.
method: The authors extend the study of breaking to general mappings, characterize 2-breaking of APN functions, introduce strongly breaking, and use a natural character transformation closely related to the sum-of-square indicator of components.
result: They prove that a 3rd-order sum-free APN function must be 3-breaking, derive structural results for the new notions, characterize a subclass of APN functions via 2-strongly breaking, and answer Open Problem 4 from IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 52(9): 4160-4170, 2006.
conclusion: The work clarifies interrelations among APN-related properties and provides a framework that captures component-wise APNness and balancedness, including for Dillon's APN permutation and Gold functions.

title: Update To: Spectral Sets: Numerical Range And Beyond
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use the results of Lorist and Schwenninger, {\em A solution to Crouzeix's conjecture}, arXiv:2608.03841v2, [URL] to update the 2019 paper of Crouzeix and Greenbaum, {\em Spectral sets: Numerical range and beyond}, SIAM J.~Matrix Anal.~Appl., 40(3):1087-1101. For all regions considered in the 2019 paper, we are able to show that the region is a [MATH]-spectral set with a bound on [MATH] that is smaller than that established in the 2019 paper. In particular, we show that various annular regions are [MATH]-spectral sets and that a more general convex region with a circular hole or cutout is a [MATH]-spectral set.
tldr: This note updates a 2019 paper on spectral sets by using a recent solution to Crouzeix's conjecture to obtain improved k-spectral set bounds for annular and other planar regions.
motivation: The authors aim to revise and strengthen earlier results on spectral sets and numerical range in light of the recent resolution of Crouzeix's conjecture by Lorist and Schwenninger.
method: They apply the results of Lorist and Schwenninger to reanalyze the regions considered in the 2019 paper, proving that various annular regions and more general convex regions with a circular hole or cutout are k-spectral sets with smaller bounds.
result: For all regions from the 2019 paper, the paper establishes improved k-spectral set bounds, including explicit improvements for annular regions and certain convex regions with a circular hole or cutout.
conclusion: The work refines and extends the theory of spectral sets for planar regions, yielding tighter constants than previously known, but it remains a contribution to operator theory and numerical linear algebra rather than quantum information.

title: Subgame Perfection In Graph Games With $\omega$-Recognizable Preference Relations
authors: V\'eronique Bruy\`ere, Christophe Grandmont, No\'emie Meunier, Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Raskin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the constrained existence problem for subgame perfect equilibria (SPEs) in multiplayer graph games. In the proposed framework, each player has a preference relation over the set of plays, assumed to be [MATH]-recognizable. Equivalently, he has a preference relation over a finite set of payoffs, and the set of plays with the same payoff is [MATH]-regular, for each payoff. This generic framework avoids the need to focus on specific payoff functions. We show that the constrained SPE existence problem is EXPTIME-complete, as well as for Nash equilibria (NEs).
tldr: The paper studies the constrained existence problem for subgame perfect equilibria in multiplayer graph games where players' preference relations are ω-recognizable, proving EXPTIME-completeness for both SPE and Nash equilibrium existence.
motivation: Classical results on equilibria in graph games often rely on specific payoff functions (e.g., mean-payoff, parity); the authors aim for a generic framework that abstracts away from particular payoff functions by using ω-recognizable preference relations.
method: Players' preferences are represented over a finite set of payoffs, with the set of plays sharing each payoff being ω-regular; the paper analyzes the computational complexity of deciding constrained existence of SPEs (and NEs) in this setting.
result: The constrained SPE existence problem is shown to be EXPTIME-complete, and the same complexity holds for Nash equilibria.
conclusion: The ω-recognizable preference framework yields a broad, payoff-agnostic characterization of equilibrium existence complexity in multiplayer graph games, generalizing prior payoff-specific results.

title: Spectral Characterization And Network Systems Dynamics Of Zero-Divisor Topologies Over $\mathbb{F}_p[x]/\langle X^4\rangle$: Consensus, Reliability, And Transport
authors: Apurba Sarkar, Kalyan Hansda, Makhan Maji
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For an odd prime [MATH], let [MATH] denote the zero-divisor graph associated with the finite local ring [MATH], having [MATH] vertices and size [MATH]. Using an equitable 4-cell partition induced by the ideal filtration [MATH], we prove that [MATH] decomposes into discrete levels [MATH] with multiplicities [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, alongside three irrational roots of an irreducible cubic polynomial [MATH], yielding adjacency energy [MATH]. In contrast, the Laplacian spectrum is entirely integral: [MATH]. Consequently, the tree entropy satisfies [MATH], with small-failure unreliability bounded by [MATH]. In linear consensus [MATH], error trajectories decouple into three modal timescales [MATH] with algebraic connectivity [MATH] and steady-state [MATH] error variance [MATH]. Furthermore, the Kirchhoff index yields a vanishing average resistance distance [MATH], while unbiased Markovian random walks induce an asymptotic traffic concentration vector [MATH] with quadratic per-node core routing stress [MATH].
tldr: The paper performs a spectral and network-dynamics analysis of the zero-divisor graph of the finite local ring F_p[x]/<x^4>, covering consensus, reliability, and transport properties.
motivation: Zero-divisor graphs are of interest in algebraic graph theory for relating ring-theoretic structure to graph spectra, and the authors aim to characterize such graphs over a specific finite local ring for network applications.
method: An equitable 4-cell partition induced by the ideal filtration is used to decompose the adjacency and Laplacian spectra into discrete levels and roots of a cubic polynomial, from which graph energies, tree entropy, consensus timescales, and random-walk quantities are derived.
result: The adjacency spectrum contains discrete levels and three irrational roots yielding a specific adjacency energy, while the Laplacian spectrum is entirely integral; the analysis gives tree entropy, small-failure unreliability bounds, algebraic connectivity, steady-state error variance, Kirchhoff index, and a traffic concentration vector.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed spectral and dynamical characterization of a particular zero-divisor graph, but it lies outside the scope of quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo For Vector Perturbation Precoding In Mu-mimo Via Continuous Relaxation
authors: Junichiro Hagiwara, Toshihiko Nishimura, Yasutaka Ogawa, Takeo Ohgane
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) is a key technology that improves wireless capacity through multiple antennas. In MU-MIMO downlink precoding, vector perturbation (VP) is a representative nonlinear method that achieves high performance. However, its search for the integer perturbation vector reduces to a closest vector problem, whose complexity grows rapidly as the number of users increases. We propose a method that relaxes the discrete structure of the integer perturbation into a continuous mixture of [MATH]-distributions, enabling efficient search via gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC). Complexity analysis and numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Its search complexity scales as O(N^2) in the number of users N. At a symbol error rate of 10^-3, it performs within 2.4 dB of a hypersphere approximation benchmark, which approximates the performance limit of VP. This paper reframes the VP perturbation search as a probabilistic inference problem, providing a general formulation for handling high-dimensional discrete search in a continuous space.
tldr: The paper proposes using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo via a continuous relaxation of the integer perturbation vector to solve the vector perturbation precoding search problem in MU-MIMO downlink systems.
motivation: Vector perturbation precoding achieves high MU-MIMO performance, but its integer perturbation search is a closest vector problem whose complexity grows rapidly with the number of users, motivating a more efficient search method.
method: The discrete integer perturbation structure is relaxed into a continuous mixture of distributions, enabling efficient gradient-based search using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, with accompanying complexity analysis and numerical experiments.
result: The proposed search scales as O(N^2) in the number of users and, at a symbol error rate of 10^-3, performs within 2.4 dB of a hypersphere approximation benchmark that approximates the VP performance limit.
conclusion: Reframing VP perturbation search as probabilistic inference in a continuous space provides a general formulation for high-dimensional discrete search in MU-MIMO precoding.

title: An LLM-Assisted AutoML Framework For Intrusion Detection In IoT Networks
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems are increasingly deployed in smart homes, transportation, energy systems, and critical infrastructure. This broad connectivity improves service intelligence, but also enlarges the attack surface of IoT networks. Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are widely used to identify malicious network threats and protect IoT systems, but developing effective ML-based IDS models often requires human expertise and repeated manual decisions on many procedures, including data pre-processing, feature selection, model selection, and hyperparameter tuning. Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) reduces this burden by automating steps of the ML pipeline using optimization techniques, but conventional AutoML methods can consume substantial optimization time because they explore broad candidate model families and large hyperparameter spaces. This paper proposes a Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted AutoML framework for IoT intrusion detection. The proposed framework uses an LLM as a policy generator that converts dataset profiles into bounded and validated AutoML policies for automated data balancing, automated feature engineering, and Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization (CASH). Under an equal 10-trial budget, the proposed LLM-assisted policy achieves higher weighted test F1-score than traditional AutoML using the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) on both datasets, reaching 99.680% on CICIDS2017 and 99.186% on IoTID20. Relative to the broader 30-trial Traditional AutoML-TPE baseline, the 10-trial proposed method reduces optimizer time by 63.7% and 49.9%, respectively, while achieving slightly higher F1-score. These results show that a bounded LLM policy can improve the quality of a low-budget AutoML search while retaining a clear efficiency advantage relative to a larger conventional search budget.
tldr: An LLM-assisted AutoML framework that uses a large language model as a policy generator to automate data balancing, feature engineering, and CASH for IoT intrusion detection.
motivation: Developing effective ML-based intrusion detection systems for IoT requires extensive human expertise and manual tuning, while conventional AutoML methods waste substantial optimization time exploring broad model families and hyperparameter spaces.
method: The framework profiles the dataset and has an LLM produce bounded, validated AutoML policies for automated data balancing, feature engineering, and combined algorithm selection and hyperparameter optimization, evaluated against a TPE-based AutoML baseline on CICIDS2017 and IoTID20.
result: Under an equal 10-trial budget the LLM-assisted policy achieved higher weighted test F1-scores (99.680% on CICIDS2017, 99.186% on IoTID20) while cutting optimizer time by 63.7% and 49.9% relative to a 30-trial TPE baseline.
conclusion: A bounded LLM-generated policy can improve low-budget AutoML search quality while retaining an efficiency advantage over larger conventional search budgets for IoT intrusion detection.

title: The Limit And Its Ground. QBism, Scientific Realism, And The Born Rule
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QBists insist that theirs is a realist position while denying that the quantum formalism represents a mind-independent world. The insistence is hard to place. The realism debate is throughout a dispute about represented content, so a theory that denies standing in the representation relation appears not to take up a position within that debate at all. This paper examines the most developed attempt to make good on the QBist claim--David Glick's perspectival normative realism--and argues that it fails instructively. Glick seeks the ground of the Born rule's objectivity among states of affairs and construes an agent's perspective as a location within an already-constituted world; finding no state of affairs fit to bind every agent at once, he must book the ground as brute. Phenomenology supplies the third thing his picture lacks. A horizon is not a position within the world but the condition under which a world is given. Read as an agent's weighting--her curvature--of such a horizon, the quantum state is neither a defective description nor a brute posit, and the Born rule articulates the invariant lawfulness by which any sense confers a curvature at all.
tldr: A philosophy-of-physics critique of QBist attempts to ground the objectivity of the Born rule, proposing a phenomenological reading of the quantum state as an agent's 'curvature' of a horizon.
motivation: QBism claims to be a realist position while denying that the quantum formalism represents a mind-independent world, and this tension with the scientific realism debate is hard to locate; the paper aims to diagnose why the most developed defense of that claim fails.
method: Conceptual and phenomenological analysis of David Glick's perspectival normative realism, arguing that searching for the ground of the Born rule among states of affairs forces it to be booked as brute.
result: The proposed alternative treats the quantum state as an agent's weighting (curvature) of a horizon—the condition under which a world is given—rather than a defective description or brute posit, with the Born rule expressing the invariant lawfulness of sense-conferring curvature.
conclusion: The paper offers a phenomenological reframing of QBism and the Born rule, contributing to interpretive philosophy of quantum mechanics rather than to technical quantum information science.

title: Intermittency In Wind-Driven Fires
authors: Laurent H\'ebert-Dufresne, Aanjaneya Kumar, S. Redner
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a wind-driven forest-fire model in one dimension in which a fire can jump gaps between trees to ignite disjoint downwind forests. The size of a gap that a fire can jump depends on the fire intensity, which increases as the fire propagates through trees and diminishes as the fire jumps gaps. Trees grow on empty sites at rate [MATH] and lightning strikes each site with rate [MATH]. When [MATH], where [MATH] is the system length, lightning is sufficiently rare that quasi-deterministic dynamics arises where all trees are consumed when a lightning-induced fire occurs. For [MATH] with [MATH], lightning is sufficiently frequent that a steady state is reached, but with unexpected behaviors for the forest- and gap-size distributions. Intermittency arises in between these regimes, with coexisting temporal domains of deterministic and chaotic dynamics.
tldr: The paper introduces a one-dimensional wind-driven forest-fire model with gap-jumping fires, revealing quasi-deterministic, steady-state, and intermittent dynamical regimes.
motivation: Forest-fire models are classic nonequilibrium statistical mechanics systems, and the authors aim to extend them to include wind-driven fire propagation that can jump gaps to ignite disjoint forest patches.
method: A one-dimensional lattice model is constructed where trees grow at rate p, lightning strikes at rate f, and fire intensity increases while propagating through trees but decays when jumping gaps, allowing analytic and numerical study of the resulting dynamics.
result: For rare lightning (f ~ 1/L) the dynamics become quasi-deterministic and consume all trees, while frequent lightning yields a steady state with unexpected forest- and gap-size distributions; between these regimes, intermittency emerges with coexisting deterministic and chaotic domains.
conclusion: Wind-driven gap-jumping introduces novel intermittent behavior and anomalous size distributions in forest-fire models, broadening the phenomenology of nonequilibrium critical systems.

title: Below The Surface: Creep, Corrosion, And Tipping Points In The Social Resilience Of Science
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By its most visible quantitative metrics: numbers of researchers, papers, journals, and institutions, science has never looked healthier. Yet a set of subsurface indicators points the other way: the disruptiveness of the average paper and patent is falling, progress slows in the largest fields, replication is rare and often unsuccessful. Incentive systems can select for poor methods even when no one is actually cheating. Lay society shows a curious mixture of admiration and lack of trust for scientists and their work. We argue that a healthy-looking surface can coexist with, and mask, an accumulation of below-the-surface damage due to slow-acting, internally and externally driven pressures, weakening the social position of science. This process is best understood not as an acute shock but as a creeping crisis. And while the damage grows slowly, it may result in a sudden collapse of the research as social institution. To make this diagnosis tractable rather than merely alarming, we import the conceptual and mathematical apparatus of two mature research fields that already study such slow degradation and sudden collapse processes: the continuum damage mechanics of creep, fatigue, and corrosion, and the ecology of resilience, regime shifts, and critical transitions. We do not claim to resolve whether science is merely robust under strain or is approaching a tipping point; the available data are too fragmentary. This remains a question of importance and we propose what would answer it: finding measurable early-warning indicators, use of agent-based models of the coupled trust-incentive-funding feedback system, understanding adversarial attacks, and the design of resilience building and recovery interventions. The result is a research agenda, and an argument for why the health of science cannot be read off its own success reports.
tldr: This paper argues that science's visible success metrics mask slow subsurface damage, and proposes borrowing concepts from creep/corrosion mechanics and resilience ecology to diagnose a possible creeping crisis and sudden institutional collapse.
motivation: The authors aim to reconcile declining disruptiveness, replication failures, and public distrust with apparently healthy quantitative indicators of science, and to frame this as a tractable systemic risk rather than mere alarm.
method: The paper imports conceptual and mathematical tools from continuum damage mechanics (creep, fatigue, corrosion) and ecological resilience theory (regime shifts, critical transitions) to interpret social and institutional trends in science.
result: No new empirical result is reported; the paper synthesizes existing indicators and proposes a research agenda including early-warning indicators, agent-based models of trust-incentive-funding feedback, adversarial attack analysis, and resilience interventions.
conclusion: The authors conclude that whether science is robust or approaching a tipping point remains unresolved due to fragmentary data, and argue that assessing the health of science requires indicators beyond its own success reports.

title: On Product Spectral Sets And Functional Tiles In $\mathbb{Q}_p^d$
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies product spectral sets and functional tiles in the [MATH]-adic spaces [MATH] within the framework of the {\bf product spectral set conjecture}. We establish a stability result for functional tiles under weak convergence of tiling complements, characterize product spectral pairs with product spectra, and fully resolve the conjecture for cylindric sets by proving that spectrality of a cylindric set [MATH] is equivalent to spectrality of [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies product spectral sets and functional tiles in p-adic spaces within the product spectral set conjecture.
motivation: The product spectral set conjecture concerns the spectrality of product sets and their tiling complements, extending classical Fuglede-type questions to p-adic settings.
method: The author establishes a stability result for functional tiles under weak convergence of tiling complements, characterizes product spectral pairs with product spectra, and resolves the conjecture for cylindric sets.
result: For cylindric sets, spectrality is proven equivalent to spectrality of a lower-dimensional projection, fully resolving the conjecture in that case.
conclusion: The work advances the product spectral set conjecture in Q_p^d, providing structural and stability results for functional tiles and product spectral pairs.

title: Admissible $qx+1$ Sequences, Semiconvergents, And Rational Catalan Numbers
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For an odd integer \(q\geq3\), let \(a_q(r)\) count finite words in \(\{q/2,1/2\}\) containing exactly \(r\) factors \(q/2\), with every proper prefix product greater than \(1\) and total product less than \(1\). For \(q=3,5,7\), these are OEIS , , and . Put \[ \alpha_q=\log_2q,\qquad m_r(q)=\lfloor r\alpha_q\rfloor. \] Using the classical cycle lemma in this \(q\)-specific setting, we recover the two natural Beatty passage bounds \[ \frac1r{r-1} \leq a_q(r)\leq \frac1r{r-1}, \] and prove their equality criteria directly. The lower and upper equality orders are the denominators of the strict lower and upper one-sided best approximations to \(\log_2q\); together they are the denominators of all convergents and semiconvergents. Equivalently, they are the strict record minima and maxima of the binary mantissas \(q^r/2^{m_r(q)}\). At every nontrivial equality order, the admissible words are in explicit bijection with rational Dyck paths, so that \(a_q(r)\) is a rational Catalan number. We also prove monotonicity in \(q\), compare the three OEIS sequences, and derive their growth constants and exact normalized oscillations.
tldr: The paper counts admissible qx+1 sequences using Beatty bounds and shows they are rational Catalan numbers at equality orders.
motivation: The author studies finite words over {q/2,1/2} with prefix-product constraints, aiming to characterize their counts and connect them to known combinatorial objects.
method: The analysis uses the classical cycle lemma and one-sided best approximations to log_2 q, with explicit bijections to rational Dyck paths.
result: The admissible counts satisfy tight lower and upper Beatty passage bounds, whose equality orders are denominators of convergents and semiconvergents to log_2 q, and at these orders the counts are rational Catalan numbers.
conclusion: The paper provides a number-theoretic and combinatorial classification of admissible qx+1 sequences, including monotonicity in q and growth constants, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: On Series Involving $\binom{4k}{k}^{-1}$
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we prove two conjectures of Sun concerning the evaluation of two series involving the reciprocal of the binomial coefficient [MATH]. The values of these series are related to [MATH], [MATH], and the Gieseking constant [MATH]. Our proofs rely on the Beta function and the Clausen function.
tldr: The paper proves two conjectures of Sun on evaluating series involving the reciprocal of the central binomial coefficient 4k choose k, expressing their values via the Clausen function and the Gieseking constant.
motivation: The conjectures by Sun regarding evaluations of series with reciprocal binomial coefficients remained unproven, and such series connect to special functions and geometric constants.
method: The proofs rely on integral representations via the Beta function along with properties of the Clausen function to evaluate the series in closed form.
result: Both conjectured series are evaluated in terms of Clausen function values and the Gieseking constant, confirming Sun's conjectures.
conclusion: The work settles open conjectures in classical number theory and illustrates the utility of Beta and Clausen function techniques for binomial reciprocal series, but has no connection to quantum information science.

title: A Proof Of The Irreducibility Conjecture For Legendre Polynomials
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the irreducibility conjecture for Legendre polynomials proposed by Stieltjes in his 1890 letter to Hermite. Assuming a nontrivial factorization, we take the differences between roots belonging to distinct factors, multiply these differences, and include the leading coefficients to obtain a nonzero integer, the resultant of the two factors. We first bound the exponent with which each odd prime divides this integer, obtaining an upper bound for its odd part. We then use an identity for derivatives at roots, derived from the Legendre differential equation, to prove that the same odd part exceeds another explicit quantity. Comparing the two bounds rules out all factorizations for original degrees [MATH]. The remaining degrees are covered by Groth's previously established finite-range result.
tldr: The paper proves Stieltjes' 1890 irreducibility conjecture for Legendre polynomials using resultant bounds and a derivative identity from the Legendre differential equation.
motivation: Stieltjes conjectured in 1890 that Legendre polynomials are irreducible over the rationals, and the problem has remained open for original degrees beyond those covered by Groth's finite-range result.
method: Assuming a nontrivial factorization, the author forms the resultant of the two factors as a nonzero integer, bounds the odd part via prime-exponent estimates, and derives a lower bound for the same odd part using a derivative identity at roots.
result: The two bounds are compared to rule out all factorizations for the remaining original degrees, completing the proof of the irreducibility conjecture.
conclusion: Legendre polynomials are irreducible over the rationals, resolving a long-standing conjecture from Stieltjes' correspondence with Hermite.

title: Finite Normal Forms And Causal Inversion For Fractional Operator Algebras
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional operator algebras provide a natural setting for linking algebraic normal forms to causal inversion, but arbitrary smooth multipliers and Volterra kernels destroy finite fractional rewriting. We construct an algebra generated by polynomial multipliers, fractional powers indexed by an additive subgroup [MATH] containing [MATH], and flat causal convolution operators. Its finite polynomially weighted diagonal-flat convolution operators form the smallest two-sided ideal containing the flat generators, polynomial multipliers are intrinsic, and distributional separation yields a unique finite normal form with an additive order filtration. For monic normal forms, the leading power selects a canonical causal right factor that extends from the flat core to the natural range [MATH]. Completing the negative-order convolution sector in [MATH] admits integrable Sonine and Prabhakar kernels, while an independently prescribed continuous bivariate Volterra term remains external. Under injectivity and power-type kernel bounds, variable lower-order terms and this bivariate perturbation reduce to one weakly singular second-kind equation, whose classical resolvent exists on every finite interval without smallness assumptions. A finite boundary-jet block incorporates prescribed initial data without changing the reduced kernel. Sonine, distributed-order, and regularized-Prabhakar realizations follow. In the noninteger Prabhakar regime, an exact range criterion characterizes the classical [MATH] subdomain, and an explicit Riemann--Liouville example proves that it is strictly smaller than the continuous natural range.
tldr: The paper constructs a fractional operator algebra with finite normal forms and studies causal inversion via Sonine and Prabhakar kernels and Volterra equations.
motivation: Fractional operator algebras provide a natural framework for linking algebraic normal forms to causal inversion, but arbitrary smooth multipliers and Volterra kernels generally destroy finite fractional rewriting.
method: The authors build an algebra generated by polynomial multipliers, fractional powers indexed by an additive subgroup, and flat causal convolution operators, then establish a unique finite normal form with an additive order filtration and reduce certain perturbations to a weakly singular second-kind equation.
result: They show that polynomial multipliers are intrinsic, a canonical causal right factor exists for monic normal forms, and completion in the negative-order convolution sector admits integrable Sonine and Prabhakar kernels, with an exact range criterion in the noninteger Prabhakar regime.
conclusion: The work provides a structural algebraic approach to finite rewriting and causal inversion for fractional operators, with realizations such as Sonine, distributed-order, and regularized-Prabhakar, but it is purely mathematical and disconnected from quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Domain-decomposed Evolutional Deep Neural Network With Random Features For Transient Pressure Diffusion With Discontinuous And High-Contrast Coefficients
authors: Peiqi Li, Jie Chen, Hui Zhang, Simon Hands
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transient pressure diffusion in heterogeneous porous media becomes difficult to resolve efficiently when permeability is discontinuous and spans several orders of magnitude. We develop a domain-decomposed random-feature evolutional deep neural network (DD RF-EDNN) that separates spatial approximation from temporal evolution. Permeability-informed random features are compressed into an orthonormal pressure space, and a conservative finite-volume operator is projected onto this space so that only the reduced coordinates are advanced in time. This formulation retains the dissipative structure of the discrete flow problem without repeated neural-network optimization. The analysis quantifies dictionary and singular-value truncation errors, proves contractivity under an energy-consistent dissipativity correction, and derives a conditional grid-level estimate for homogeneous dynamics and time-independent data admitting a steady lifting. Experiments on low-permeability inclusions, high-conductivity channels and blocks, and three-dimensional grids demonstrate consistent accuracy across distinct coefficient structures. The method reaches a final-time relative [MATH] error of [MATH] in the principal benchmark and maintains errors on the order of [MATH] at a permeability contrast of [MATH]. Numerical diagnostics further show that the observed error balance and temporal convergence are consistent with the analysis. These results support DD RF-EDNN as a structure-preserving and interpretable reduced formulation for transient simulations on prescribed heterogeneous media.
tldr: The paper develops a domain-decomposed random-feature evolutional deep neural network for transient pressure diffusion in heterogeneous media with discontinuous and high-contrast permeability.
motivation: Transient pressure diffusion in heterogeneous porous media is difficult to resolve efficiently when permeability is discontinuous and spans several orders of magnitude.
method: The method separates spatial approximation from temporal evolution using permeability-informed random features compressed into an orthonormal pressure space, with a conservative finite-volume operator projected onto this space for reduced-coordinate time advancement.
result: The analysis quantifies truncation errors, proves contractivity under an energy-consistent dissipativity correction, and demonstrates accurate results on low-permeability inclusions, high-conductivity channels, and three-dimensional grids.
conclusion: DD RF-EDNN is supported as a structure-preserving and interpretable reduced formulation for transient simulations on prescribed heterogeneous media.

title: Exact Maximum Likelihood Inference For Drifted Multi-sub-fractional Brownian Motion At Discrete Observation
authors: Afrah Al-Harby, Ezzedine Mliki, Manal Al-Ohali
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sub-fractional Brownian motion is self-similar and long-range dependent but has no stationary increments, so the increment covariance is not Toeplitz and no spectral density is available. We show that a complete finite-sample likelihood theory survives nonetheless. The model is a linear trend observed at [MATH] equidistant times through a superposition of [MATH] independent sub-fractional Brownian motions with known Hurst indices and a common scale. Nondegeneracy follows from realising the process as the even part of a two-sided fractional Brownian motion, and the maximum likelihood estimators of the trend and of the scale are explicit. The statistics on which inference rests are pivotal, their laws depending on the sample size alone, so intervals and tests of exact level are available at every [MATH], together with complete sufficiency, minimum variance unbiasedness and attainment of the Cram\'er--Rao bound. An explicit variance bound gives strong consistency and asymptotic normality, and simulations confirm the exact coverage and the predicted effect of a misspecified Hurst vector.
tldr: The paper develops exact finite-sample maximum likelihood inference for a linear trend observed discretely from a superposition of independent sub-fractional Brownian motions with known Hurst indices and a common scale.
motivation: Sub-fractional Brownian motion is self-similar and long-range dependent but lacks stationary increments, so standard spectral and Toeplitz covariance methods do not apply.
method: The process is represented as the even part of a two-sided fractional Brownian motion, yielding explicit maximum likelihood estimators for the trend and scale and pivotal statistics whose distributions depend only on sample size.
result: The estimators are complete sufficient, minimum variance unbiased, attain the Cramér–Rao bound, and give exact-level confidence intervals and tests; simulations confirm exact coverage and robustness to a misspecified Hurst vector.
conclusion: A complete finite-sample likelihood theory is possible for this non-stationary long-range dependent model despite the absence of a spectral density.

title: Fairly Compensated Distributed Information Retrieval And Augmentation For Ai Agents
authors: Yixiang Yao, Pasha Barahimi, Srivatsan Ravi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing reliance of autonomous AI agents on external and distributed knowledge sources introduces a fundamental challenge for decentralized information marketplaces: retrieval agents must evaluate the quality and relevance of data before purchase, while data providers must avoid revealing valuable information prior to guaranteed compensation. This paradox becomes particularly critical in trustless multi-agent environments, where no centralized intermediary can enforce fairness between parties. In this paper, we propose a fairly compensated protocol for distributed information retrieval and augmentation in autonomous agent networks. Our framework enables retrieval agents to securely evaluate and rank candidate documents without learning their plaintext contents, while ensuring that data providers are compensated only when valid information is successfully delivered. We further analyze the security properties of the protocol against malicious adversaries and evaluate its practical feasibility through implementations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed design is practical with current cryptographic infrastructures while preserving confidentiality, correctness, integrity, and fairness. We believe such mechanisms provide an important cryptographic foundation for trustworthy and economically sustainable decentralized knowledge marketplaces for future AI agent ecosystems.
tldr: The paper proposes a cryptographic protocol for fairly compensated distributed information retrieval and augmentation among autonomous AI agents in trustless marketplaces.
motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly rely on decentralized knowledge sources, but retrieval agents need to evaluate data quality before purchase while providers need compensation guarantees, creating a fairness paradox without a trusted intermediary.
method: The authors design a protocol enabling retrieval agents to securely evaluate and rank candidate documents without learning plaintext contents, while ensuring providers are compensated only upon valid delivery, with security analysis against malicious adversaries.
result: Implementations and experiments show the design is practical with current cryptographic infrastructures while preserving confidentiality, correctness, integrity, and fairness.
conclusion: The work provides a cryptographic foundation for trustworthy and economically sustainable decentralized knowledge marketplaces for future AI agent ecosystems.

title: Beyond A Single Optimal Design: A Dynamical Systems Characterization Of Online Allocation With Convex Costs
authors: Haoxin Sang, Bo Sun, Xiaoqi Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online allocation with convex costs (\OACC), a generalization of limited-supply models in which additional resources can be produced dynamically at convex cost. Prior work largely focuses on constructing a single algorithm that achieves strong competitive guarantees. In contrast, our main contribution is a structural characterization of the optimal design space of reserve functions (i.e., normalized pricing rules) for \OACC, yielding a family of optimal online algorithms. Using a principled dynamical-systems approach, we show that optimal online algorithms arise as solutions of a nonlinear eigenvalue problem: the optimal competitive ratio corresponds to the dominant eigenvalue, and the associated eigenfunction determines the optimal reserve function. This perspective establishes the existence of infinitely many optimal designs attaining the best possible competitive ratio, thereby unifying and generalizing a broad class of prior algorithms. Beyond unification, our characterization uncovers new structural phenomena, including the ability to flexibly mix dynamic and static pricing without loss of optimality and the construction of universally competitive algorithms under unknown or stochastic costs. We further extend the analysis to more structured settings such as supply-oblivious arrivals and hard supply constraints, obtaining sharper guarantees that improve upon previous bounds.
tldr: The paper derives a dynamical-systems characterization of the optimal design space of reserve functions for online allocation with convex costs, showing optimal algorithms correspond to solutions of a nonlinear eigenvalue problem.
motivation: Prior work on online allocation with convex costs focuses on constructing a single algorithm with good competitive guarantees, leaving the broader structure of optimal pricing/reserve rules unexplored.
method: The authors use a principled dynamical-systems approach, reducing optimal online algorithm design to a nonlinear eigenvalue problem whose dominant eigenvalue gives the optimal competitive ratio and whose eigenfunction gives the optimal reserve function.
result: They show infinitely many optimal designs attain the best competitive ratio, unifying and generalizing prior algorithms, and uncover phenomena such as lossless mixing of dynamic and static pricing plus universally competitive algorithms under unknown or stochastic costs, with sharper bounds for supply-oblivious arrivals and hard supply constraints.
conclusion: The framework provides a structural characterization that unifies existing online allocation algorithms and yields new families of optimal designs, extending to more constrained settings with improved guarantees.

title: Two-Stage Refinement Sparse Channel Estimation For Reconfigurable Intelligent Metasurface Antenna (rimsa) Massive Mimo
authors: Yakun Ma, Hui-Ming Wang, Jiaping He, Qingli Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To meet the increasing demands for high data rates and large capacity, next generation wireless communication systems require transceivers equipped with a large number of antennas. Massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) with metasurface antennas has emerged as a promising solution. In this paper, we investigate the channel estimation problem for the emerging reconfigurable intelligent metasurface antenna (RIMSA) array systems. Specifically, we develop a two-stage refinement (TSR) channel estimation method based on the compressed sensing (CS) principle. In the first stage, we exploit the antenna structure of RIMSA to receive pilots by setting identical phase response vectors across all RIMSAs. In this manner, the coherence of the measurement matrix under the CS framework is reduced and the channel estimation performance is improved. However, this special design introduces channel direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation ambiguity and yields an ambiguous candidate DoA set. In the second stage, we optimize the phase responses of the metamaterial elements to resolve the ambiguity and accurately estimate the DoAs and channel coefficients. Overall, the estimation accuracy is improved in the first stage at the cost of ambiguity, and this ambiguity is eliminated in the second stage. We illustrate the performance advantages of the TSR method by presenting the numerical results and comparing it with the existing methods.
tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage refinement compressed-sensing method for channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent metasurface antenna (RIMSA) massive MIMO systems.
motivation: Next-generation wireless systems need large antenna arrays, and RIMSA massive MIMO is promising but suffers from challenging channel estimation due to high dimensionality and measurement matrix coherence.
method: A two-stage refinement (TSR) approach is developed: first, identical phase response vectors across RIMSAs reduce measurement matrix coherence but introduce DoA ambiguity; second, metamaterial phase responses are optimized to resolve the ambiguity and estimate DoAs and channel coefficients.
result: Numerical results show improved estimation accuracy and performance advantages over existing methods.
conclusion: The TSR method effectively balances coherence reduction and ambiguity resolution for RIMSA massive MIMO channel estimation.

title: Assessing Runtime Electromagnetic Detection Of Cpu Hardware Trojans Targeting Kernel Memory
authors: Athanasios Moschos, Baki Berkay Yilmaz, Kevin Valakuzhy, Angelos D. Keromytis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Side-channels are a promising approach for hardware trojan detection, as they can passively reveal malicious hardware activity without requiring additional circuitry or destructive analysis of the device under test. This work investigates the use of electromagnetic (EM) emanations for runtime detection of hardware trojan attacks. Using an open-source hardware trojan that implements an arbitrary memory-write primitive, we tamper with the kernel memory of a Linux system running on a RISC-V microarchitecture and perform a real-time baseline detection using the processor's EM emissions. Our results indicate that, under certain conditions, hardware trojans can be detected indirectly through the anomalous software behavior they enable.
tldr: This paper investigates runtime detection of CPU hardware trojans that tamper with Linux kernel memory using electromagnetic (EM) side-channel emanations on a RISC-V platform.
motivation: Hardware trojans are difficult to detect because they can be inserted during fabrication and remain dormant; side-channels offer a passive, non-destructive detection route that avoids added circuitry and destructive analysis.
method: The authors deploy an open-source hardware trojan implementing an arbitrary memory-write primitive into a RISC-V Linux system, then perform real-time baseline detection by monitoring the processor's EM emissions during kernel-memory tampering.
result: The measurements show that, under certain conditions, EM emanations allow indirect detection of hardware trojans via the anomalous software behavior they induce, though detection is conditional rather than universal.
conclusion: EM side-channel monitoring can serve as a practical, passive complement to existing hardware trojan detection methods, but its reliability depends strongly on operating conditions.

title: Suboptimality Loss For Inverse Learning From Imperfect Equilibria
authors: Andreas Feik, Pierre Pinson, Dario Paccagnan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many modern systems involve the strategic interaction of multiple agents. In such settings, observed actions typically reflect equilibrium behavior under utilities that are only partially known. Recovering these hidden utilities from data - the central goal of inverse game theory - is key for prediction, counterfactual analysis, and mechanism design. However, existing approaches based on inverse variational inequalities are highly sensitive to noisy and inconsistent equilibrium observations, thus limiting their applicability. In this paper, we resolve this issue by introducing a game-theoretic suboptimality loss that measures the aggregate utility gain players could obtain by unilaterally deviating from an observed strategy profile. First, we show that this loss is convex and admits an efficient decomposition into player-wise best-responses. Second, we show this loss is sandwiched between the predictability loss and the inverse variational inequality loss, making it a tractable surrogate for equilibrium prediction. Third, we develop a mirror descent algorithm to minimize it and demonstrate on a heterogeneous networked Cournot competition that our approach remains accurate under noisy observations and inconsistent equilibrium data while inverse variational inequality methods produce degenerate estimates.
tldr: The paper introduces a game-theoretic suboptimality loss for inverse learning from imperfect equilibrium observations, with convexity, decomposition, and mirror descent algorithms.
motivation: Inverse game theory aims to recover hidden utilities from observed strategic actions, but existing inverse variational inequality methods are sensitive to noisy and inconsistent equilibrium data.
method: The authors define a suboptimality loss measuring aggregate unilateral utility gain and show it is convex, decomposes into player-wise best responses, and is sandwiched between predictability loss and inverse variational inequality loss; they optimize it via mirror descent.
result: On a heterogeneous networked Cournot competition, the approach remains accurate under noisy observations and inconsistent equilibrium data, whereas inverse variational inequality methods produce degenerate estimates.
conclusion: The suboptimality loss provides a tractable and robust surrogate for equilibrium prediction in inverse game theory, improving applicability under imperfect data.

title: Online Wideband Mimo Channel Reconstruction From Periodically Swept RBs Via Incremental Cp Updates
authors: Boxin Huang, Libin Zheng, Minru Bai, Yuhao Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic resource-block (RB) scanning leaves most of the current wideband channel unobserved and mixes measurements of different ages. We develop an online canonical polyadic tracker with proximal block updates (CP-PBCD) that reconstructs the full channel after each narrow-RB acquisition. Age-weighted finite histories, frequency and temporal regularization, and bounded component management maintain an adaptive low-rank representation. Two warm-started conjugate-gradient iterations and parallel shifted frequency solves provide a fixed per-frame update budget. Training-user spatial projection strengthens noise suppression at low pilot SNR. Experiments cover ten test users, three speeds, four SNRs, and complete 1000-frame trajectories with 1-ms RB acquisition. Direct first-RB CP-PBCD achieves lower mean normalized mean squared error (NMSE) than all six baselines in all twelve conditions. At 3.6 km/h and 20 dB, it improves on periodic physical refitting by 3.91 dB and runs 35.1 times faster, averaging 0.717 ms per online update. Optional dispersed startup pilots improve early acquisition, while a controlled initialization study yields a last-100-frame NMSE range of 0.427 dB across pilot budgets. These results demonstrate accurate current-channel reconstruction through incremental updates with submillisecond average computation.
tldr: An online canonical polyadic (CP) tensor tracker with proximal block updates reconstructs wideband MIMO channels incrementally from periodically swept resource blocks, achieving sub-millisecond per-frame updates and lower NMSE than six baselines.
motivation: Periodic RB scanning in wideband MIMO systems leaves most of the channel unobserved and mixes measurements of different ages, motivating a fast online reconstruction scheme.
method: The authors develop CP-PBCD, an age-weighted, regularized online CP decomposition with bounded component management, warm-started conjugate-gradient iterations, parallel shifted frequency solves, and training-user spatial projection for noise suppression.
result: Across ten users, three speeds, four SNRs, and 1000-frame trajectories, direct first-RB CP-PBCD attains lower mean NMSE than all six baselines in all twelve conditions, improving on periodic physical refitting by 3.91 dB while running 35.1x faster (0.717 ms per update).
conclusion: Incremental CP updates enable accurate, low-latency current-channel reconstruction for wideband MIMO systems, with optional dispersed startup pilots improving early acquisition.

title: Toward Well-Posed Problems In The Social Sciences: Hadamard's Criteria As Epistemic Guardrails
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an interdisciplinary framework for evaluating the epistemic robustness of social-scientific inquiry through Hadamard's criteria for well-posed problems: existence, uniqueness, and stability. Reinterpreting these criteria not as demands for deterministic certainty but as methodological guardrails, we show how they diagnose recurrent failures of identification and inference across quantitative and qualitative paradigms. In quantitative research (e.g., econometric modeling), instability manifests when substantive conclusions depend sensitively on model specifications or data filtering. In interpretivist qualitative research, non-uniqueness and non-falsifiability arise when theoretical frameworks are elastic enough to accommodate contradictory observations without pre-specified rejection criteria. We frame these failures as inverse problems where the mapping from empirical data to substantive claims fails to satisfy existence, uniqueness, or stability. Finally, we propose cross-paradigmatic safeguards: ex-ante falsification criteria, empirical boundary conditions, multiverse sensitivity auditing, and cross-observer validation, to ensure social-scientific claims remain appropriately constrained, falsifiable, and robust to perturbations in evidence and interpretation.
tldr: The paper proposes using Hadamard's criteria for well-posed problems (existence, uniqueness, stability) as methodological guardrails to diagnose and remedy epistemic failures in quantitative and qualitative social science research.
motivation: Social-scientific inquiry frequently suffers from fragile identification and inference, where conclusions depend on arbitrary model specifications or unfalsifiable interpretive frameworks, and the authors seek a unifying diagnostic for these failures.
method: The authors reinterpret Hadamard's criteria as non-deterministic epistemic guardrails and cast social-scientific inference as an inverse problem, analyzing failure modes across econometric modeling and interpretivist qualitative research, then proposing cross-paradigmatic safeguards such as ex-ante falsification criteria, empirical boundary conditions, multiverse sensitivity auditing, and cross-observer validation.
result: The framework shows that instability in quantitative work and non-uniqueness/non-falsifiability in qualitative work both map onto violations of Hadamard's existence, uniqueness, or stability conditions, and that the proposed safeguards can constrain claims against perturbations in evidence and interpretation.
conclusion: Hadamard's criteria can serve as a general epistemic scaffold for making social-scientific research problems better posed and more robust, independent of the quantitative/qualitative divide.

title: Contour Computation Of Linearized Painlev\'e Ii And Iv Solutions With Monodromy-Based Error Control
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the numerical evaluation of contour integral representations for solutions of the linearized second and fourth Painlev\'e equations. The construction combines a nonlinear background solution, continuation of canonical Lax-pair columns, normalization matching, and quadrature over cycles with decaying branches in distinct sectors. Accuracy is assessed using a reference fundamental matrix, differential-equation residuals, and variations of monodromy data computed independently from the spectral problem. An exact identity describes the propagation of initial-basis errors. A stagewise a posteriori refinement criterion uses increments in monodromy variations to allocate numerical accuracy. The contour algorithm is compared with the Dormand--Prince method on a regular background, in a region of rapid solution growth, and through hard loss of stability followed by approximately regular oscillations. Accumulated offsets in monodromy variations and subsequent drift are measured separately. The experiments show how drift depends on spectral conditioning, quadrature accuracy, and error allocation between initial and subsequent parts of the computation. Five additional initial-data and parameter cases demonstrate the dependence of comparative performance on the nonlinear background.
tldr: The paper develops a contour-integral numerical algorithm for solving linearized Painlevé II and IV equations, using monodromy variations as an a posteriori error-control criterion.
motivation: Solutions of linearized Painlevé equations are needed in applications ranging from integrable systems to random matrix theory, but their reliable numerical evaluation in regions of rapid growth and instability is difficult.
method: The algorithm combines a nonlinear background solution, continuation of canonical Lax-pair columns, normalization matching, and quadrature over cycles with decaying branches in distinct sectors, with accuracy assessed via a reference fundamental matrix, differential-equation residuals, and independently computed monodromy data.
result: Comparisons with the Dormand–Prince method across regular, rapidly growing, and stability-losing regimes show that accumulated offsets in monodromy variations and subsequent drift depend on spectral conditioning, quadrature accuracy, and error allocation between initial and later stages.
conclusion: A stagewise a posteriori refinement criterion based on monodromy-variation increments enables adaptive accuracy allocation, and the approach is validated across five additional initial-data and parameter cases.

title: Selections Of Set-Valued Maps Under Stieltjes Clocks: Regularity, Variation, And Atomic Structure
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Stieltjes clock allows effective time to advance continuously, remain unchanged over intervals, or jump. We study whether a compact-valued set-valued map evolving relative to a Stieltjes clock admits a single-valued selection that passes through a prescribed graph point while retaining the regularity and variation of the multifunction. For g-H\"older exponents [MATH], we prove that regularity can be preserved without increasing the g-H\"older seminorm, with no monotonicity assumption on g. If g is additionally nondecreasing, one prescribed-point selection preserves both this regularity and the Hausdorff variation on every subinterval. The same selection consequently preserves all finite Riesz p-variations associated with nondecreasing external clocks. For [MATH], the structure becomes jump-driven. For left-continuous nondecreasing Stieltjes clocks, continuous clock evolution cannot generate variation: all variation is carried by jumps. We obtain exact jump decompositions for both the set-valued map and its selection, together with explicit atomic formulas for Riesz p-variation. Examples show that the principal regularity, variation, and jump bounds are attained. For compact-convex Euclidean-valued maps, we also examine the case [MATH]. In this setting, the H\"older exponent can still be preserved, but preservation of the same constant through a prescribed point holds in one dimension and can fail in higher dimensions. Finally, without a quantitative H\"older bound, we characterize exactly when every compact-valued Hausdorff g-continuous map admits a prescribed-point g-continuous selection: precisely when the clock image is zero-dimensional.
tldr: The paper studies existence and regularity of single-valued selections of compact-valued set-valued maps evolving under Stieltjes clocks, focusing on preservation of Hölder regularity, Hausdorff/Riesz variation, and jump decompositions.
motivation: Stieltjes clocks allow effective time to advance continuously, stay constant, or jump, raising the question of whether a multifunction's regularity and variation can be retained by a prescribed-point selection.
method: The authors prove selection theorems using g-Hölder seminorms, Hausdorff variation, Riesz p-variation, and explicit jump/atomic decompositions; they also analyze compact-convex Euclidean-valued maps via dimension arguments.
result: Regularity can be preserved without increasing the g-Hölder seminorm; under nondecreasing g, a single selection preserves both regularity and variation; left-continuous nondecreasing clocks produce jump-driven variation, and higher-dimensional constant preservation can fail.
conclusion: The paper characterizes exactly when a prescribed-point g-continuous selection exists for all compact-valued Hausdorff g-continuous maps, namely when the clock image is zero-dimensional, and gives examples attaining the bounds.

title: Differentially Private And Fairness-Audited Score Diffusion For Irregular Longitudinal Health Records
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharing irregular longitudinal health records can accelerate model development, yet synthetic releases may leak participation, distort temporal dependence, suppress rare events, or reduce utility for underrepresented groups. We present TRUST LONGSYNTH, an auditable patient level private generator that combines bounded sufficient statistics, zCDP accounted Gaussian releases, conditional analytic score diffusion, block banded temporal covariance, separate missingness and gap models, and a protected event sampling floor with population weights. The method was evaluated on five independently generated, three cohort benchmarks containing 720 patients, fourteen irregular observation slots, six mixed variables, informative missingness, and a rare deterioration outcome. At epsilon = 12 and delta = 10 to the power of minus 5, TRUST LONGSYNTH achieved mean train synthetic test real AUPRC 0.342, Brier score 0.088, expected calibration error 0.082, correlation error 0.222, autocorrelation error 0.317, and membership attack AUROC 0.499. Relative to the private diagonal score baseline, AUPRC increased by 7.5 percent, while Brier, calibration, correlation, and autocorrelation errors decreased by 6.1 percent, 17.0 percent, 28.0 percent, and 30.1 percent, respectively. The method did not dominate every nonprivate or discrete baseline, and corrected paired tests were inconclusive with five seeds. Canary exposure was 1.8 percent, compared with 28.8 percent for DP Score in the same stress test. These findings support a transparent privacy utility fairness evaluation protocol, not clinical validity or unconditional release safety, and motivate governed external validation on real multi site records.
tldr: TRUST LONGSYNTH is a differentially private generator for irregular longitudinal health records that aims to preserve temporal dependence, rare events, and fairness while providing auditable privacy guarantees.
motivation: Sharing longitudinal health records can advance modeling, but synthetic releases risk privacy leakage, distorted temporal structure, suppressed rare outcomes, and reduced utility for underrepresented groups.
method: The approach combines bounded sufficient statistics, zCDP-accounted Gaussian releases, conditional analytic score diffusion, block-banded temporal covariance, separate missingness and gap models, and protected event sampling with population weights.
result: At epsilon=12 and delta=1e-5, it achieved AUPRC 0.342, Brier 0.088, calibration error 0.082, correlation error 0.222, autocorrelation error 0.317, and membership attack AUROC 0.499, with canary exposure 1.8% compared with 28.8% for DP Score.
conclusion: The findings support a transparent privacy-utility-fairness evaluation protocol but not clinical validity or unconditional release safety, motivating governed external validation on real multi-site records.

title: Defusing Explosive Prompts: Understanding And Preventing Trigger-Based Prompt Injections In Llm Agents
authors: Justin Szczepaniak, Elad Feldman, Naum Viner, Ben Nassi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM applications integrate with external tools, they are increasingly exposed to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions are embedded in retrieved content. Conventional IPIs fire on contact: the moment an agent ingests the content, it carries out the instruction. We introduce the explosive prompt, a conditional payload that stays dormant until an attacker-chosen trigger is met, in effect a training-free, inference-time backdoor planted in a single piece of retrieved content. This temporal separation reaches where ordinary IPI cannot. On frontier models that refuse the bare imperative almost entirely, rephrasing the same goal as a dormant conditional drives real, state-changing tool execution against a live agent backend (a paired mean of 16.5% vs. 2.4% for the imperative, reaching 34.2% on a proprietary model). In trials on nine production agents (OpenAI Codex, Google Gemini CLI, Anthropic Claude Code CLI, Cursor CLI, GitHub Copilot, Devin AI CLI, Amazon Kiro CLI, Qwen Code, Google Assistant; n=30 each), explosive prompts succeed in 43-83% of cases versus at most 3% for an imperative baseline, and they slip past deployed defenses: off-the-shelf injection classifiers are miscalibrated on them, and a preference-optimized model that closes imperative injection entirely still executes 11.8% of explosive prompts, every one at the trigger turn. The durable defensive lever is ingestion-time detection of the conditional structure, once detectors are trained on explosive-prompt data, which no prior benchmark supplied and our generator does. Retraining cuts live tool-execution attack success from an undefended 34.3% to 7.5-8.1% for the encoder baselines. Our detector, DeFuse, reaches 3.0% at a calibrated 5% false-positive budget with the best detection quality of any method tested (AUC 0.9994) and 25x lower latency, though it needs length-aware thresholds.
tldr: The paper introduces 'explosive prompts', a training-free, inference-time conditional prompt-injection payload that stays dormant until an attacker-specified trigger, and shows it bypasses deployed defenses on nine production LLM agents.
motivation: Indirect prompt injection normally fires immediately when an agent ingests retrieved content, so defenders focus on ingestion-time detection of imperative instructions; the authors ask whether delaying the payload to a trigger event can evade those defenses.
method: They design a generator producing conditional (trigger-based) payloads, benchmark them against imperative baselines on frontier models and nine production agents (n=30 each), evaluate off-the-shelf injection classifiers and a preference-optimized defense model, and train an encoder-based detector (DeFuse) on their new data.
result: Explosive prompts achieve 43-83% success across production agents versus at most 3% for imperative baselines, and still succeed 11.8% against a preference-optimized defense; retraining detectors cuts live tool-execution success from 34.3% to 7.5-8.1%, with DeFuse reaching 3.0% at a 5% false-positive budget (AUC 0.9994).
conclusion: Conditional, temporally separated prompt injections are a distinct and effective attack class, and ingestion-time detection of conditional structure trained on explosive-prompt data is the durable defense.

title: Kernel-Checked Frontier Certificates For Erd\H{o}s Problem 414
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH], where [MATH] counts divisors. Erds and Graham asked, after Spiro, whether the orbits of any two positive integers under [MATH] eventually share a point (Problem 414 on Bloom's list). The problem is open, and a finite computation cannot close it; nothing about it has been checked by a proof kernel, and the statement in the formal-conjectures repository carries a sorry. We replay what can be certified through the Lean 4 kernel under an axiom gate (axioms exactly propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no sorry; no native_decide). Three elementary facts recorded by Li, namely that coalescence is an equivalence relation, [MATH] is odd exactly for squares, and [MATH] is bounded by [MATH] so that orbits skip no square annulus [MATH], are formalized, and his frontier lemma is formalized in a window form: every orbit started below a level [MATH] has a point within [MATH] below [MATH]. The frontier lemma becomes a certificate: the [MATH] values [MATH] just below [MATH] and the orbit points above [MATH] until the orbits through the crossing points have merged. Its soundness is a kernel-checked theorem, and the certified rungs state that every pair of positive integers below [MATH] coalesces for [MATH]; the certificate at [MATH] has 44,530 entries rather than [MATH]. Every ledger and every quoted count was produced by two programs sharing no code that agree by hash. We record what is known about a non-coalescing pair and measure the exit-set sizes Li bounds. Nothing here is a proof of the conjecture.
tldr: A Lean 4 formalization effort certifying elementary, kernel-checked facts and a frontier certificate for the open Erdős Problem 414 on divisor iterates, without proving the conjecture.
motivation: Erdős and Graham's Problem 414 (whether the iterated divisor-sum orbits of any two positive integers eventually coalesce) remains open, and no machine-checked partial result existed in the formal-conjectures repository, which carries a 'sorry'.
method: The author formalizes Li's elementary lemmas (coalescence as an equivalence relation, oddness of f(n) exactly for squares, square-annulus skipping bounds) in Lean 4 under a strict axiom gate (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound; no sorry, no native_decide), and recasts the frontier lemma as a finite certificate verified across two independent programs agreeing by hash.
result: The soundness of the frontier certificate is a kernel-checked theorem, and certified rungs show all pairs of positive integers below the stated bounds coalesce; the certificate at one level has 44,530 entries, and exit-set sizes are measured.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous kernel-verified partial certificates around an open number-theoretic problem but explicitly does not constitute a proof of the conjecture, and lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

Using the canonical remainder operator [MATH], we identify the two local residue classes excluded by each prime [MATH]. Their possible collision is characterized exactly by [MATH]. An inclusion--exclusion argument combined with the Chinese remainder theorem gives an exact formula containing at most [MATH] terms. We prove that the associated finite correlation has cardinality [MATH] and obtain the affine identity [MATH]. We also establish an exact finite-density decomposition with uniform error smaller than [MATH], a half-period positivity theorem, and a product-cutoff criterion.
