title: Asymptotics And Finite Sample Bounds For Prediction And Smoothing In Wright-Fisher Hidden Markov Models
authors: Luigi M. Malgieri, Filippo Ascolani, Matteo Giordano, Matteo Ruggiero
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models with a latent signal given by a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion and discrete-time categorical observations, motivated by repeated-sampling time-series settings, including temporally binned ancient-DNA data, in which noisy frequency counts are recorded at finitely many times. Our focus is on the exact Bayesian predictive and smoothing distributions available under parent-independent mutation, in relation to their large-sample targets under repeated within-time sampling. For a fixed collection-time grid and diverging within-time sample sizes, we show that the exact Wright-Fisher predictive and smoothing distributions converge in total variation to the corresponding population transition and bridge laws at the limiting neighboring frequencies. We then derive explicit finite-sample control for the predictive law and a corresponding finite-sample bound for the marginal smoother. Finally, at the inspection times, we show that the joint conditional law concentrates at the target frequencies and that its active coordinates are asymptotically Gaussian, while coordinates with zero true frequencies converge to Gamma limits at faster rates. Our regime imposes no restriction on dependence across inspection times beyond within-time sampling. The analysis rests on a fixed-interval tail bound for Kingman's coalescent block-counting process, which is of independent interest.
tldr: The paper establishes asymptotic and finite-sample convergence bounds for Bayesian prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models whose latent signal is a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion.
motivation: Repeated-sampling time-series data, such as temporally binned ancient-DNA frequency counts, motivate the need for exact Bayesian predictive and smoothing distributions and a rigorous understanding of their large-sample behaviour.
method: Under parent-independent mutation, the authors prove total-variation convergence of exact Wright-Fisher predictive and smoothing laws to population transition and bridge laws as within-time sample sizes diverge, using a fixed-interval tail bound for Kingman's coalescent block-counting process.
result: They obtain explicit finite-sample control for the predictive law, a finite-sample bound for the marginal smoother, and show the joint conditional law concentrates at target frequencies with Gaussian asymptotics for active coordinates and Gamma limits for zero-frequency coordinates.
conclusion: The results provide a rigorous statistical foundation for prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher HMMs without restricting dependence across inspection times, and the coalescent tail bound is of independent interest.

title: Trace Formula For Billiard Flow On Surfaces With Concave Boundary
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study grazing closed trajectories of the billiard flow [MATH] on a compact surface [MATH] with concave boundary. Under a non-degeneracy condition, which is satisfied for example when [MATH] has negative sectional curvature, we compute the trace of a regularized pullback [MATH] near a closed trajectory grazing once, which is an analogue of the Atiyah--Bott--Guillemin trace formula for closed billiard trajectories.
tldr: The paper derives a trace formula for the billiard flow on compact surfaces with concave boundary, computing the trace of a regularized pullback near a once-grazing closed trajectory as an analogue of the Atiyah–Bott–Guillemin trace formula.
motivation: Trace formulas for billiard flows are central tools in spectral geometry and semiclassical analysis, but the grazing-trajectory regime on concave-boundary surfaces has remained poorly understood.
method: Under a non-degeneracy condition (e.g., negative sectional curvature), the authors analyze closed billiard trajectories that graze the boundary once and compute the trace of a regularized pullback operator near such trajectories.
result: They obtain a trace formula for grazing closed trajectories parallel to the Atiyah–Bott–Guillemin formula for closed geodesics.
conclusion: The result extends trace-formula technology to billiard flows on surfaces with concave boundary, contributing to spectral geometry and quantum-classical correspondence for billiard systems.

title: Strategic Opinion Manipulation In Multiplex Networks
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Models of opinion dynamics on networks, provide a framework to study how a network of agents aggregates dispersed opinions into a consensus. However, existing models assume that agents truthfully report their opinions, and do not account for environments in which a platform aggregates agents' reports across multiple networks, and agents can strategically report different opinions on each. In this paper, we propose a model of strategic opinion manipulation on multiplex networks, in which a platform merges L network layers with attention weights, and each agent, holding a private opinion, chooses (potentially different) reports on each layer, at a layer-specific misreporting cost, so as to pull the merged consensus toward their own opinion. We show that this game has a unique Nash equilibrium in closed form, that the resulting consensus is the truthful consensus under a centrality tilted toward a manipulability index of each agent, and that the resulting distortion is the (centrality-weighted) covariance of agents' manipulability and opinions. We further show that agents' reports on every layer are more extreme than their opinions, so that the polarization observed by the platform overestimates the true polarization. Notably, we highlight that merging layers is a double-edged sword: as manipulability depends on the square of an agent's influence on each layer, spreading attention across layers dilutes manipulation, while heterogeneous misreporting costs across layers and shifts in agents' centralities can amplify it. Finally, we characterize the platform's optimal choice of attention weights, in closed form when the layers share a stationary distribution, and through an exact gradient and a marginal test otherwise. Together, our findings shed light on when aggregating opinions across networks is (not) robust to strategic manipulation, and point out potential interventions to alleviate it.
tldr: The paper models strategic opinion manipulation on multiplex networks where agents misreport opinions across layers to influence a merged consensus.
motivation: Existing opinion dynamics models assume truthful reporting and ignore environments where platforms aggregate reports across multiple networks and agents can strategically misreport on each layer.
method: The authors formulate a game with L network layers, attention weights, and layer-specific misreporting costs, deriving a unique closed-form Nash equilibrium and analyzing the platform's optimal attention weights.
result: The equilibrium consensus equals the truthful consensus under a centrality tilted by a manipulability index, distortion is the centrality-weighted covariance of manipulability and opinions, and reports are more extreme than private opinions, overestimating polarization.
conclusion: Merging layers is double-edged: spreading attention dilutes manipulation, while heterogeneous costs and centrality shifts can amplify it; the findings inform when aggregation is robust and potential interventions.

title: Zero-Trust Authorization And Discovery For Enterprise Mcp
authors: Huan Li, Yuwei Wang, Srinivasan Manoharan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents translate natural-language context, which may include attacker-controlled text, into privileged tool calls, so authorization must remain effective even when an agent is prompt-injected or adversarially steered. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become a widely adopted interface for this boundary, yet its official SDKs' authentication and authorization primitives fall short of enterprise zero-trust requirements, most acutely a dual-persona model in which one server must serve human users (corporate SSO) and automated agents (service-account credentials on a different header). We conduct a systematic gap analysis of six surveyed MCP SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, Swift) and identify three structural shortcomings: credential extraction bound to a single Authorization header, complicating dual-persona deployment without custom middleware; the absence of pre-authentication tool discovery; and the lack of fine-grained per-tool authorization in the base SDKs. We close these gaps with composable extensions to FastMCP: cross-header credential normalization for enterprise deployments serving both human and service-account callers, cached token verification across heterogeneous IdPs, an unauthenticated metadata endpoint for credential-free registry discovery, and permission-filtered tool visibility kept consistent with per-tool invocation enforcement by a single declarative annotation, all without modifying the protocol or SDK internals. Across four frontier LLMs over 2160 attempts, an in-body-check-only server still exposes forbidden tools (152/720, 21.1%), whereas permission-aware visibility drives the rate to 0/720; visibility-only filtering remained bypassable by scripted clients, while models referenced the hidden tool by name in up to 94% of settings when inferable from the prompt, confirming that discovery controls cannot replace invocation-time enforcement.
tldr: A security engineering paper that identifies authorization and discovery gaps in official Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDKs and proposes composable FastMCP extensions for enterprise zero-trust deployments serving both human users and automated LLM agents.
motivation: LLM agents convert attacker-influenceable natural-language context into privileged tool calls, so authorization must hold even under prompt injection; existing MCP SDK authentication primitives fail enterprise zero-trust requirements, notably the dual-persona case of corporate SSO users plus service-account agents.
method: Systematic gap analysis of six MCP SDKs (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, C#, Swift) identifying three structural shortcomings, followed by composable FastMCP extensions: cross-header credential normalization, cached token verification across heterogeneous IdPs, an unauthenticated metadata discovery endpoint, and permission-filtered tool visibility tied to per-tool invocation enforcement via a single declarative annotation.
result: Across 2160 attempts with four frontier LLMs, an in-body-check-only server exposed forbidden tools in 152/720 cases (21.1%), whereas permission-aware visibility reduced this to 0/720; visibility-only filtering remained bypassable by scripted clients, and models named hidden tools in up to 94% of settings when inferable from the prompt.
conclusion: Discovery-time controls cannot substitute for invocation-time enforcement; the proposed extensions close the identified gaps without modifying the MCP protocol or SDK internals, enabling zero-trust authorization for enterprise agent deployments.

title: LLMs As Linguistic Chameleons: Decoupling Semantics And Structure For Privacy-Preserving Communication
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) APIs become increasingly integrated into privacy-sensitive workflows, ensuring inference-time privacy without compromising task utility remains a major challenge. Existing approaches preserve most of the original semantic content to maintain downstream performance, but this also leaves exploitable cues for reconstructing the original text. This work investigates semantic decoupling, which replaces original semantics with alternative content while preserving the structure needed for LLM reasoning. Based on this idea, we propose CROSS-MAP, a bidirectional framework that maps private inputs into a different semantic domain before inference and recovers the corresponding outputs afterward. Local models are trained with multi-objective optimization to maximize semantic divergence in the mapping stage while minimizing semantic inconsistency in the recovery stage. Experiments show that CROSS-MAP reduces reconstruction success across multiple attack settings while outperforming existing baselines in utility.
tldr: CROSS-MAP is a bidirectional framework that replaces private input semantics with an alternative semantic domain before LLM inference and then recovers outputs, aiming to preserve utility while resisting text reconstruction attacks.
motivation: LLM APIs are increasingly used in privacy-sensitive workflows, and existing privacy methods retain too much original semantics, leaving cues that allow reconstruction of the original private text.
method: The authors propose semantic decoupling, training local models via multi-objective optimization to maximize semantic divergence in the forward mapping stage while minimizing semantic inconsistency in the recovery stage.
result: Experiments show CROSS-MAP reduces reconstruction success across multiple attack settings while outperforming existing baselines on downstream utility.
conclusion: Semantic decoupling offers a practical route to inference-time privacy for LLM-based workflows without sacrificing task performance.

title: Security Of Agent-Integrated Software: When Human Operations And Agent Actions Coexist
authors: Ding Yang, Yuchen Ling, Shengcheng Yu, Zhenyu Chen, Chunrong Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent-Integrated Software (AIS) embeds an intelligent agent in a conventional application, supporting both human operations and agent actions. Human operations let users make precise changes and inspect results, while agent actions carry out routine or multi-step tasks. These complementary roles make coexistence a likely long-term feature of many software systems. Human operations and agent actions affect the same software state and can use one another's results. Therefore, security policies must remain effective across both paths. We argue that AIS security must be assessed at the level of the whole software system. Protecting the agent and the conventional software core separately does not establish that they are secure together. To guide security analysis of AIS as a whole, we organize the problems arising from this coexistence into four categories: context misuse, authorization violation, execution control, and effect integrity. Using these categories, we examine how current practices address the security problems in AIS and where their protection remains limited. Building on this analysis, we identify research opportunities in preserving information provenance, enforcing policy across operation paths, maintaining valid authorization over time, and managing persistent effects and recovery. This resulting perspective provides a conceptual framework for understanding and improving the security of AIS.
tldr: The paper proposes a conceptual framework for analyzing the security of Agent-Integrated Software (AIS), where human operations and autonomous agent actions share the same software state.
motivation: Intelligent agents are increasingly embedded in conventional applications, and since human operations and agent actions act on the same state and can consume each other's outputs, security must be evaluated for the whole system rather than for the agent and core separately.
method: The authors organize the security problems arising from human-agent coexistence into four categories—context misuse, authorization violation, execution control, and effect integrity—and use them to survey how current practices address (or fail to address) these issues.
result: The analysis identifies limitations in existing protection approaches and highlights research opportunities in information provenance, cross-path policy enforcement, time-valid authorization, and management of persistent effects and recovery.
conclusion: AIS security should be treated as a system-level property, and the proposed taxonomy offers a conceptual framework for understanding and improving it.

title: Cloader: Evading Security Mobile Defenses Via Runtime Obfuscation And Adaptive Hooking Tactics
authors: Nhat-Anh Huynh, Minh Quang Luu, Ngoc Hong Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a stealth framework that eliminates detection of hooking tools such as Frida and Xposed in secured mobile environments by replacing static configurations with dynamic evasion tactics. In contrast to existing approaches that apply these techniques independently, the framework introduces a unified runtime control layer that systematically coordinates network, temporal, and code-level evasive transformations. The solution integrates randomized port allocation, runtime code obfuscation, delayed execution triggers, and self-integrity checks to disrupt signature-based scans, timing heuristics, and tampering attempts. A custom Android loader, CLoader, enforces these mechanisms to isolate hooking activities from security monitors while maintaining complete interception and modification capabilities. Validation across enterprise anti malware systems, hardened applications, and device management platforms demonstrates a 90% bypass rate in our evaluation matrix. This approach enables reliable penetration testing and malware analysis in locked-down mobile ecosystems by masking network, temporal, and code-level fingerprints without architectural overhauls.
tldr: CLoader is an Android runtime obfuscation and adaptive hooking framework that evades mobile security defenses, achieving a 90% bypass rate in enterprise anti-malware and hardened app environments.
motivation: Security researchers and penetration testers need reliable ways to instrument mobile applications in locked-down environments, where hooking tools like Frida and Xposed are routinely detected and blocked.
method: The framework combines randomized port allocation, runtime code obfuscation, delayed execution triggers, and self-integrity checks into a unified runtime control layer enforced by a custom Android loader called CLoader.
result: Validation across enterprise anti-malware systems, hardened applications, and device management platforms demonstrates a 90% bypass rate while preserving full interception and modification capabilities.
conclusion: CLoader shows that coordinating network, temporal, and code-level evasive transformations can reliably evade mobile security defenses without architectural overhauls, aiding penetration testing and malware analysis.

title: Cohomology Of $\mathfrak{psl}(n|n)$ In Trivial And In Adjoint Representations
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compute the cohomology of the projective special linear Lie superalgebra [MATH] over a field of characteristic zero in trivial and in adjoint coefficients in full detail through its associated Hochschild--Serre spectral sequences. Applications in physics exist for its real form, the projective special unitary Lie superalgebra [MATH] --- in particular, [MATH] for AdS/CFT. We also find the cohomology of [MATH] in trivial coefficients along the way and we point out a discrepancy with a previous statement in the literature. We present the explicit cohomology groups of low degree for [MATH].
tldr: The paper computes the cohomology of the projective special linear Lie superalgebra psl(n|n) in trivial and adjoint representations using Hochschild-Serre spectral sequences, with mention of AdS/CFT applications.
motivation: The cohomology of Lie superalgebras is of mathematical interest, and the real form psu(n|n) has applications in physics, particularly in AdS/CFT correspondence.
method: The author employs Hochschild-Serre spectral sequences to systematically compute the cohomology groups in trivial and adjoint coefficients, and also derives the cohomology of a related algebra in trivial coefficients.
result: Explicit cohomology groups in low degrees are presented for psl(n|n), and a discrepancy with a previous statement in the literature is pointed out.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed computation of cohomology for psl(n|n) and corrects a known result, potentially useful for mathematical physics in the context of AdS/CFT.

title: Asymptotic Invariance Of Kelly Allocation Under Power-Law Asset Dynamics: Evidence From Bitcoin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine log-optimal portfolio allocation when the long-run price of an asset follows a power-law trajectory, [MATH], and its instantaneous return variance decays as [MATH]. Under a zero risk-free-rate benchmark, the continuous-time Kelly fraction scales as [MATH]. Exact temporal invariance therefore occurs when [MATH], whereas deviations from this value produce systematic age dependence in the allocation. We propose a scaling hypothesis connecting growth in network participation, effective market liquidity, and declining volatility. Under a specified set of scaling assumptions, this model predicts the benchmark exponent [MATH]. Using historical daily Bitcoin prices, we estimate the power-law price exponent and examine the sensitivity of the volatility exponent to the length of the rolling window. For windows of four to nine years, the estimated volatility exponents have an arithmetic mean of 0.53 and a cross-window standard deviation of approximately 0.03. Because these estimates are obtained from overlapping observations and the same underlying price history, this spread is interpreted as a measure of model sensitivity rather than a formal confidence interval. Finally, we show that a time-dependent multiplicative contribution to return variance generally breaks exact Kelly invariance. We illustrate this result using a scenario in which Bitcoin transaction-fee variability affects the effective variance process. The results identify the conditions under which log-optimal allocation can remain stable under non-stationary power-law asset dynamics and clarify the assumptions required when applying this result to Bitcoin.
tldr: The paper analyzes log-optimal Kelly allocation for an asset following a power-law price trajectory and decaying volatility, using Bitcoin as a case study.
motivation: It aims to understand when Kelly portfolio allocations remain stable under non-stationary power-law asset dynamics and to connect network participation, liquidity, and volatility scaling.
method: The authors derive continuous-time Kelly fraction scaling under power-law price and volatility decay, propose a scaling hypothesis for the benchmark exponent, and estimate power-law exponents from historical daily Bitcoin prices using rolling windows.
result: Exact temporal invariance occurs when the volatility exponent equals a specific benchmark value; Bitcoin estimates yield a mean volatility exponent of 0.53 with cross-window standard deviation around 0.03, and time-dependent multiplicative variance breaks exact invariance.
conclusion: The conditions for stable log-optimal allocation under power-law dynamics are identified, and the assumptions required for applying the model to Bitcoin are clarified.

title: Distributional Fractional Taylor Series And Interpretation Of The Fractal And Number-Theoretic Explicit Formulas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the work of M. L. Lapidus and M. van Frankenhuisjen on fractal explicit formulas for generalized fractal strings, we develop in this paper a distributional fractal Taylor's formula with error term and an exact distributional fractal Taylor series representation for generalized fractal strings. The explicit formulas that the aforementioned authors developed provide a way of expressing a generalized fractal string [MATH] in terms of the underlying fractal complex dimensions, under suitable growth assumptions on its geometric zeta function, [MATH], known as the languidity assumptions. This involves a sum indexed by the complex dimensions of the generalized fractal string, summing over all residues of [MATH], multiplied by the Mellin transform of a tempered or Schwartz test function [MATH], denoted by [MATH]. Under languidity assumptions, there is an error term present. In this paper, we express the residue term in the fractional distributional explicit formulas as the fractional [MATH]-ordered distributional derivative of the Dirac [MATH] distribution, denoted by [MATH], applied to modified test functions of the form [MATH], where [MATH] runs from [MATH] to the multiplicity of the pole [MATH] of [MATH]. motivation: Motivated by Lapidus and van Frankenhuijsen's work on fractal explicit formulas for generalized fractal strings, the paper aims to extend these formulas through distributional fractional Taylor expansions involving fractal complex dimensions.
method: Uses distribution theory, Mellin transforms, geometric zeta functions, Laurent expansions, gamma functions, and fractional distributional derivatives applied to modified test functions.
result: Derives a distributional fractal Taylor formula with error term and an exact distributional fractal Taylor series under strong languidity, with coefficients determined by the principal part of the Laurent expansion of the geometric zeta function times the gamma function.
conclusion: Contributes to the broader program of characterizing fractals in terms of fractal Taylor series expansions involving their underlying fractal complex dimensions.

title: 1729 In The Mirror: Reversal And Affine Multiplication
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The decimal reversals 1729 and 9271 have multiplicative orders of [MATH] equal to 36 and 63. Motivated by this symmetry, we classify the affine commutation equation [MATH], where [MATH] reverses base-[MATH] digits, for every [MATH], [MATH], the classification gives an exact digit criterion for reversal of their orders. Finally, an exhaustive computation with independently checkable primality certificates proves that [MATH] is the unique pair of distinct odd decimal reversals whose orders of [MATH] are distinct two-digit reversals of each other.

motivation: The authors are motivated by the numerical symmetry that decimal reversals 1729 and 9271 have multiplicative orders 36 and 63, which are themselves two-digit reversals.

conclusion: The work provides a complete classification of order reversal under digit reversal and establishes a unique decimal example, but it is purely number-theoretic and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics research.

title: On The Unified Generalized $q$-Stirling Matrices And Their Matrix Decompositions
authors: Amerah M. Dibagulun, Charles B. Montero, Mahid M. Mangontarum
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, the unified generalized [MATH]-Stirling matrices are defined in terms of the [MATH]-analogues of the unified generalized Stirling numbers. Several matrix relations involving these matrices are derived, and matrix decompositions of the unified generalized [MATH]-Stirling matrices are established.
tldr: The paper introduces unified generalized q-Stirling matrices and derives matrix relations and decompositions for them.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the theory of unified generalized Stirling numbers to a matrix setting via q-analogues, providing algebraic tools for combinatorial and matrix-theoretic applications.
method: They define q-Stirling matrices in terms of q-analogues of unified generalized Stirling numbers and derive matrix relations, then establish matrix decompositions of these matrices.
result: Several matrix relations are derived and matrix decompositions of the unified generalized q-Stirling matrices are established.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic matrix-theoretic framework for generalized q-Stirling numbers, extending classical combinatorial identities to matrix form.

title: A Quadratic Critical-value Conjecture For The Fifth Bessel Moment
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We conjecture an explicit evaluation of the pure fifth Bessel moment [MATH] as a quadratic expression in the critical value [MATH] of the weight-three, level-60 newform [MATH] (LMFDB orbit 60.3.b.a) identified in the twisted fifth-moment modularity theorem of Lim, Tu and Yu, with coefficients in [MATH] and the square taken before the real part. Directed interval computations, using no stored Bessel or [MATH]-values, bound the absolute discrepancy by [MATH]. We prove two exact modular identities for [MATH]: the Petersson-norm formula [MATH] and the coefficient-conjugation relation [MATH] with explicit [MATH]. We also record the exact relation [MATH] between the even and odd determinants of Lim, Tu and Yu, as a consequence of Chuang's period formulas, and distinguish their symmetric-square conjecture for [MATH] from the individual-period formula proposed here. The Bessel-to-modular equality remains conjectural. Verification programs are included as ancillary files.
tldr: The paper conjectures a quadratic expression for the pure fifth Bessel moment in terms of the critical value of a weight-three level-60 newform and provides numerical interval verification.
motivation: Bessel moments are known to connect to modular forms and L-values, and the authors aim to extend such modularity relations to the fifth moment.
method: The work states an explicit conjectural identity, uses directed interval computations to bound the discrepancy, and proves exact modular identities including a Petersson-norm formula and a coefficient-conjugation relation.
result: The conjecture relates the fifth Bessel moment to the square of the real part of a critical L-value, with absolute discrepancy bounded numerically, and also records an exact relation between even and odd determinants.
conclusion: The Bessel-to-modular equality remains conjectural, but supporting modular identities and verification programs are supplied.

title: A Proof Of The Common Root Conjecture For Legendre Polynomials
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove Stieltjes' common root conjecture: Legendre polynomials of distinct degrees have no common nonzero root. We construct an auxiliary polynomial and show that, for the relevant power of two [MATH], the edge of slope [MATH] in its [MATH]-adic Newton polygon has horizontal length less than [MATH]. If a common nonzero root existed, Newton polygon theory and the Legendre differential equation would force the same edge to have horizontal length at least [MATH], yielding a contradiction.
tldr: The paper proves Stieltjes' common root conjecture that Legendre polynomials of distinct degrees have no common nonzero root.
motivation: The conjecture is a classical open problem in the theory of orthogonal polynomials and special functions.
method: The author constructs an auxiliary polynomial and analyzes a 2-adic Newton polygon, showing a certain edge has horizontal length less than 1, while assuming a common root would force the same edge to have length at least 1.
result: The contradiction proves that no common nonzero root can exist for Legendre polynomials of distinct degrees.
conclusion: This settles the common root conjecture for Legendre polynomials.

title: A Note On A Recent Claimed Proof Of The Irrationality Of Catalan's Constant

motivation: The author examines a recent preprint claiming a proof that Catalan's constant is irrational and tests the validity of its bounding method.
method: Exact integer and rational computations are used to check the paper's rank theorem, denominator bounds, and the asymptotic ledger in its Sections 6–9.

title: Root-of-Unity Sections Of Dilated Euler-Product Quotients
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study root-of-unity sections of quotients formed from dilated Euler products. At the boundary point \(q=1\), odd sections tend to nonzero cyclotomic constants, whereas even sections have infinitely many simple real poles. We determine the locations, spacing, and residues of all sufficiently late poles. In the cubic case we find the leading oscillatory error in an elementary approximation and prove that its exponential scale is sharp. At the origin we determine exact contact, including a gap-dependent parity law, and integral divisibility with the first nonzero coefficient determined for every modulus \(|k-1|\ge2\). For Euler powers \(k\ge2\), a moving formal pole controls the section error at small fixed nomes; a real zero-free interval gives a further convergence regime. For the twenty-fourth power we prove explicit CM approximation bounds and a signed asymptotic as the dilation increases.
tldr: The paper studies root-of-unity sections of quotients formed from dilated Euler products, analyzing their boundary behavior at q=1, pole structure, and CM approximation bounds.
motivation: To understand the analytic and asymptotic properties of dilated Euler-product quotients at special points, including cyclotomic constants and pole spacing.
method: Analytic number theory and complex analysis techniques are used to locate poles, compute residues, derive oscillatory error estimates, and prove sharp exponential scales.
result: Odd sections tend to nonzero cyclotomic constants while even sections have infinitely many simple real poles; exact contact and divisibility laws are determined, and explicit CM approximation bounds are proved for the twenty-fourth power.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed pole and asymptotic analysis of these Euler-product sections, with sharp error bounds and convergence regimes for Euler powers.

title: Bernstein Constraint Complexes For Multivariate Splines On Triangulated Surfaces
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Bernstein constraint complexes, a representation of finite element differential complexes in which every triangle of a triangulation keeps its own Bernstein--B\'ezier coefficients and global continuity is imposed only through smoothness functionals attached to edges and vertices. Continuity of scalar splines, tangential continuity of spline vector fields, normal continuity of spline vector fields, and higher smoothness differ only in the edge functionals. No global basis is constructed. The structural result is a coefficient-level commuting identity: on every edge the smoothness functionals of a Bernstein derivative are explicit combinations of the smoothness functionals of its argument, through univariate Bernstein difference matrices. This gives a local proof that the kernels of the smoothness matrices form a subcomplex, for the de Rham traces and for componentwise [MATH] spline profiles, and a computable row-space test for candidate smooth profiles. We realize the lowest-order Powell--Sabin exact sequence in this form and confirm its exactness by ranks. The constrained Galerkin problem is solved in the broken coefficients with exact smoothness equations; we prove equivalence with the conforming method, treat semidefinite element operators through a pseudoinverse interface system, and give a singular pencil whose finite spectrum is the constrained Maxwell spectrum. Under the covariant and contravariant surface Piola maps the reference functionals of the de Rham sequence transfer unchanged to conforming curved triangulations. Experiments compare the null-space method, the augmented Lagrangian iteration of Awanou, Lai and Wenston, and direct solution of the saddle system on the same problems, and cover planar source and eigenvalue problems, a [MATH] biharmonic solve, the exact sphere, and an embedded hyperboloid.
tldr: Introduces Bernstein constraint complexes for finite element differential complexes on triangulated surfaces, representing splines via local Bernstein-Bézier coefficients with edge and vertex smoothness functionals.
motivation: To provide a local coefficient-level representation and commuting identities for conforming spline spaces without constructing a global basis, enabling exact sequence realization and constrained Galerkin solution.
method: Uses univariate Bernstein difference matrices to express smoothness functionals of derivatives, proves kernels form subcomplexes for de Rham traces, and solves the constrained Galerkin problem in broken coefficients with pseudoinverse and saddle-point systems.
result: Realizes the lowest-order Powell-Sabin exact sequence, confirms exactness by ranks, proves equivalence with the conforming method, treats semidefinite element operators, and reports numerical experiments on planar, spherical, and hyperboloid problems.
conclusion: The framework offers a computable, local approach to multivariate spline complexes on triangulated surfaces, with potential applications in finite element exterior calculus and surface PDEs.

title: Fitness, Predictability And Equilibrium In Biological Dynamics
authors: Rolando Rebolledo (universidad de Valpara\'iso), Mauricio Tejo (universidad de Valpara\'iso), Mara A. Freilich (brown University), Pablo Marquet
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding eco-evolutionary dynamics presents significant mathematical challenges, particularly regarding predictability, equilibrium, and the mathematical representation of fitness. Using Open System Dynamics and Stochastic Analysis, we develop a theoretical framework to characterize fitness change and its relationship with predictability. We explore the limiting behavior of biomass abundances modeled by stochastic processes, deriving continuous-time diffusion counterparts from discrete-time models. Focusing on neutrality and the search for equilibrium, we analyze diffusions in two distinct state spaces. For relative abundances on a d-dimensional simplex, we demonstrate the central role of orthogonal polynomials in model construction. For non-proportional abundances in the positive orthant of d-dimensional space, we detail two specific families of models. Finally, we address statistical inference by presenting numerical examples for relative abundances, illustrating how orthogonal polynomials facilitate maximum likelihood parameter estimation.
tldr: The paper develops a stochastic open-system framework for eco-evolutionary dynamics, focusing on fitness, predictability, and equilibrium in biological populations.
motivation: Understanding eco-evolutionary dynamics poses mathematical challenges in representing fitness and predictability, and linking discrete and continuous population models.
method: It uses open system dynamics and stochastic analysis to derive continuous-time diffusion limits from discrete models, analyzing relative and non-proportional abundances via orthogonal polynomials and maximum likelihood inference.
result: The framework characterizes fitness change and its relation to predictability, showing the central role of orthogonal polynomials on the simplex and detailing model families in the positive orthant with numerical inference examples.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical foundation for studying equilibrium and neutrality in biological dynamics, with potential applications in ecological and evolutionary modeling.

title: Descartes' Circle Theorem, Princess Elizabeth, And Spinors
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, on Descartes' famous "circle theorem," we first attempt to explain how the philosopher could have arrived at the equation that he presents without demonstration in a letter to Princess Palatine Elizabeth of Bohemia in November 1643 (a previously unpublished proof, to our knowledge). Then we report some stages of the subsequent generalization of this theorem, whose Cliffordian flavor, via the equivalence of a quadratic form and the square of a linear form, still mobilizes mathematicians today. This statement, which, over time, has undergone different extensions, Euclidean and non-Euclidean, has found, {\it in fine}, a spinor formalization. We see there the proof of what we may call, in a Bachelardian style, an "inductive value" of the truth, which extends by successive generalizations. We conclude, more briefly, with the contacts between Elizabeth and Descartes, and the perhaps symbolic meaning of these considerations on "kissing circles," as they are called in Anglo-Saxon countries, in the context of their correspondence on the soul and the body, and the question of passions.
tldr: A historical and mathematical study of Descartes' circle theorem, tracing its origins in Descartes' 1643 letter to Princess Elizabeth of Bohemia through to its modern spinor formalization.
motivation: The author aims to reconstruct how Descartes could have derived the circle theorem equation without proof, and to trace the theorem's successive generalizations as an illustration of an 'inductive value' of mathematical truth.
method: Historical-philosophical analysis of Descartes' correspondence combined with a survey of mathematical generalizations of the theorem, including Euclidean, non-Euclidean, and Clifford-algebraic/spinor formulations.
result: A previously unpublished (to the author's knowledge) reconstruction of Descartes' derivation is offered, along with a narrative of the theorem's extension culminating in a spinor formalization.
conclusion: The theorem's evolution is presented as evidence for a Bachelardian 'inductive value' of truth, closing with speculation on the symbolic meaning of 'kissing circles' in Descartes and Elizabeth's correspondence on soul, body, and passions.

title: Expanders Prevent Property (h)
authors: Bruno de Mendon\c{c} Braga, Chris Gartland, Gilles Lancien, Pavlos Motakis, Eva Perneck\'a, Thomas Schlumprecht
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that if a sequence of expander graphs equi-coarsely embeds into a Banach space, then this Banach space fails Kasparov and Yu's Property (H). Consequently, no Banach space with Property (H) can be coarsely universal for all countable groups. We provide a Lean verification of our results.
tldr: The paper shows that equi-coarse embeddings of expander graphs into Banach spaces imply failure of Kasparov and Yu's Property (H), with consequences for coarse universality of countable groups, and includes a Lean formalization.
motivation: Property (H) is an analytic property of Banach spaces tied to the coarse embeddability of expanders and to the coarse Baum-Connes conjecture. The authors aim to clarify the obstruction that expanders pose for Banach spaces with this property.
method: They prove a geometric-functional-analytic theorem: if a sequence of expander graphs equi-coarsely embeds into a Banach space, then that space does not have Property (H). The proof is accompanied by a Lean verification.
result: No Banach space with Property (H) can be coarsely universal for all countable groups. This strengthens the link between expander embeddings and failure of Property (H).
conclusion: The work provides a new obstruction for coarse universality of Banach spaces and demonstrates the use of formal verification in this area of mathematics.

title: Certified Residual Quasi-Newton Methods For Distributed Variational Inequalities
authors: Ewsey R. Obzherin, Roman M. Mozhaev, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Artem A. Agafonov, Dmitry I. Kamzolov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Second-order methods for smooth monotone variational inequalities reach the optimal rate [MATH], but a distributed exact Jacobian costs [MATH] times more communication than an operator value. We show that similarity does part of the work for free: if the server's Jacobian differs from the global one by at most [MATH], using it gives [MATH] at first-order communication cost. A quasi-Newton approximation of the residual Jacobian [MATH], built from secants already communicated, improves the model but cannot remove the [MATH] term, because any uniform bound on the Jacobian error leaves it in the rate. We therefore certify the surrogate only along the candidate step: one Jacobian-vector product tests it, and a failed test is reused as an exact correction. This attains the exact rate [MATH] while transmitting only vectors. Experiments on LIBSVM and synthetic instances measure accuracy against communication.
tldr: The paper develops certified residual quasi-Newton methods for distributed variational inequalities, achieving optimal second-order convergence rates while communicating only vectors.
motivation: Distributed exact Jacobian computation incurs high communication cost, so the authors seek to attain the optimal rate for smooth monotone variational inequalities without transmitting full matrices.
method: They use a similarity-based surrogate Jacobian and a quasi-Newton approximation built from communicated secants, then certify the surrogate along the candidate step via a Jacobian-vector product test that can be reused as an exact correction.
result: The proposed method attains the exact optimal rate for smooth monotone variational inequalities while transmitting only vectors, and experiments on LIBSVM and synthetic instances measure accuracy against communication.
conclusion: Certifying the surrogate only along the candidate step overcomes the fundamental barrier of uniform Jacobian error bounds, enabling communication-efficient second-order distributed optimization.

title: Combinatorial Optimization Augmented Machine Learning For Dynamic Electric Autonomous Dial-a-Ride Problem
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study introduces a decision-epoch-based dynamic electric autonomous dial-a-ride problem (Dyn-EADARP), in which incoming requests are collected and processed at periodic decision epochs. A key decision is not only how to serve requests, but also when to dispatch them. At each decision epoch, the service provider decides which requests to serve and which to postpone, while jointly determining vehicle routes, schedules, and charging decisions. Unexecuted parts of existing plans can be revised as new information becomes available. To solve this problem, we develop an ML--CO policy following the combinatorial optimization augmented machine learning (COAML) framework, which combines a statistical model with a combinatorial optimization layer for decision making. The statistical model predicts prizes for available requests, and a prize-collecting E-ADARP uses these prizes to jointly determine request selection, routing, scheduling, and charging. The statistical model is trained directly to improve the decisions produced by the optimization layer. Computational experiments on 320 test instances demonstrate the efficiency of ML--CO, which solves instances with nearly 500 requests in about 6 seconds on average. It achieves 8.7%--14.3% lower objective values than benchmark policies and an average gap of 4.8% to the anticipative reference. The results provide several managerial insights. First, serving requests immediately is not always best, as selectively postponing some requests can create better ride-sharing opportunities. Second, revising existing plans preserves operational flexibility and substantially improves solution quality. Finally, more frequent decision making does not necessarily improve performance, highlighting the importance of choosing an appropriate decision frequency.
tldr: This paper develops a combinatorial optimization augmented machine learning policy for a dynamic electric autonomous dial-a-ride problem, jointly deciding request selection, routing, scheduling, and charging.
motivation: The authors aim to address dynamic ride-sharing with electric autonomous vehicles, where incoming requests must be accepted or postponed at decision epochs while respecting routing and charging constraints.
method: They combine a statistical model that predicts request prizes with a prize-collecting electric autonomous dial-a-ride optimization layer, training the statistical model end-to-end to improve the resulting decisions.
result: On 320 test instances, the method solves near-500-request cases in about 6 seconds on average and achieves 8.7%–14.3% lower objective values than benchmark policies, with a 4.8% average gap to an anticipative reference.
conclusion: The study shows that selective postponement, plan revision, and appropriate decision frequency can improve dynamic electric autonomous dial-a-ride operations, while more frequent decisions are not always beneficial.

title: Scalable Incremental Robustness Analysis Of Neural Network Feedback Systems
authors: Zichen Wang, Peter Seiler, Geir Dullerud, Bin Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semidefinite programming (SDP) certificates for feedback systems containing deep neural networks (NNs) typically scale with the total number of neurons, whereas small-gain tests are scalable but can be highly conservative. This paper develops a unified and scalable framework for incremental robust stability and performance analysis of feedback interconnections involving high-dimensional NNs and unmodeled dynamics. By combining a structured decomposition of the full-order SDP condition with scalable Lipschitz constant estimation algorithms, we derive reduced verification conditions that certify incremental convergence and incremental [MATH]-gain bounds. The dimensions of the resulting control-analysis linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) depend only on the widths of the last two network layers and are . The framework preserves the coupling between the plant and the NN, with the incremental small-gain condition recovered as a special case. To further reduce conservatism, we develop a multi-round alternating update scheme that iteratively refines the coupling variables while preserving scalability. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art incremental [MATH]-gain bounds for large-scale NN feedback systems.
tldr: The paper develops a scalable SDP/LMI framework for incremental robust stability and performance analysis of feedback systems containing high-dimensional neural networks.
motivation: Standard SDP certificates for neural network feedback systems scale poorly with neuron count, while small-gain tests are scalable but overly conservative.
method: The authors combine a structured decomposition of the full-order SDP condition with scalable Lipschitz constant estimation and a multi-round alternating update scheme to obtain reduced verification conditions.
result: The resulting LMI dimensions depend only on the widths of the last two network layers, and numerical experiments achieve state-of-the-art incremental L2-gain bounds for large-scale NN feedback systems.
conclusion: The framework preserves plant–NN coupling, recovers incremental small-gain as a special case, and enables scalable robust analysis of neural network feedback interconnections.

title: Visibility Design And Strategic Reasoning
authors: Raman Ebrahimi, Sepehr Ilami, Babak Heydari, Isabel Trevino, Massimo Franceschetti
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dashboards, feeds, and leaderboards determine whom agents believe they are playing against. We study how such information architectures shape strategic behavior, and how a designer who controls them can use visibility as a lever. We propose a behavioral model in which a transparency parameter governs how selectively agents are exposed to opponents of nearby reasoning depth, and embed it in a Cognitive Hierarchy environment, which provides a tractable language for tying agents' beliefs about the sophistication of others to what they see. We show that because the exposure operator is an exponential tilt of the type distribution, the effect of transparency on aggregate behavior has a closed form: the derivative of the aggregate action with respect to [MATH] is proportional to the population-average variance of perceived sophistication. This identity signs the effect in games of strategic complements (opacity raises aggregate effort) and in coordination environments (opacity lowers the mean action), and an ordinal version holds for any response rule that is monotone in the belief. Notably, under a Poisson prior, opacity acts as a sophistication multiplier: every reasoner plays as if the population were [MATH]. We use this structure to characterize the disagreement-versus-level tradeoff faced by a coordination-minded designer, to identify the reasoning depths that respond most to visibility, and to show that opacity imposes a ``sophistication tax'' under which the deepest reasoners can lose to moderate ones. Simulations in which agents see only a noisy leaderboard of published actions reproduce both the reversal and the tax. Together, our findings highlight that who an agent sees, and not only how deeply it reasons, shapes strategic behavior, and point to visibility as a design lever.
tldr: The paper studies how visibility (transparency) in information architectures affects strategic behavior in games, showing that opacity can increase or decrease aggregate effort depending on game type.
motivation: To understand how the design of information architectures (dashboards, leaderboards) influences strategic reasoning and behavior.
method: A behavioral model with a transparency parameter embedded in a Cognitive Hierarchy environment, deriving closed-form effects on aggregate action.
result: The derivative of aggregate action with respect to transparency is proportional to variance of perceived sophistication, leading to different effects in strategic complements vs coordination games, and a 'sophistication tax'.
conclusion: Visibility is a design lever that shapes strategic behavior, and opacity can have nuanced effects on reasoning depths and outcomes.

title: Strategic Classification Has A Missing Lever: Audit Risk
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strategic classification studies how a decision maker should choose a classifier when the agents being classified can adjust their features in response to it. In existing models, the classifier is the only instrument available to the decision maker, and therefore a feature that is predictive but easy to fake can only be down-weighted or discarded. However, in many settings the decision maker can also verify: lenders verify income, admissions offices check documents, and tax authorities audit returns. In this paper, we propose a model of strategic classification in which the firm jointly designs a linear classifier and an , which assigns to each fakeable feature a probability of detection and a penalty when caught. We show that under linear costs, the classifier affects the audit problem only through the distribution of gaming rents it induces, so that the joint design problem decomposes into the choice of a score rule and an audit allocation problem. We use this decomposition to characterize the optimal audit allocation, to identify when the allocation problem is tractable and when it is NP-hard (namely, when agents can game through overlapping features under an inspection cap), and to bound the regret of a firm that has to learn the rents by auditing. We further show that audit intensity is a quantity to be tuned rather than maximized: welfare is single-peaked in it, and a firm and a social planner disagree on the mix of detection and penalty that delivers a given level of deterrence. Notably, two populations with identical costs and causal structure can game in one domain and improve in the other, a difference that a cost-only model cannot account for. Together, our findings highlight that whether a feature is ``gameable'' depends on the institution's verification policy as much as on the feature itself.
tldr: The paper proposes a model of strategic classification in which a decision maker jointly designs a linear classifier and an audit mechanism that assigns detection probabilities and penalties to fakeable features.
motivation: Existing strategic classification models treat the classifier as the only instrument available, so predictive-but-gameable features can only be down-weighted or dropped; in practice institutions can also verify claims (lenders verify income, tax authorities audit returns).
method: The authors decompose the joint classifier-and-audit design under linear costs, showing the classifier influences the audit problem only through the induced distribution of gaming rents, reducing the problem to a score rule plus an audit allocation problem; they analyze tractability, NP-hardness under overlapping features with an inspection cap, and regret bounds for learning rents by auditing.
result: They characterize the optimal audit allocation, show welfare is single-peaked in audit intensity, and demonstrate that a firm and a social planner disagree on the detection-versus-penalty mix; two populations with identical costs and causal structure can differ in gameability purely due to verification policy.
conclusion: Whether a feature is 'gameable' depends on the institution's verification policy as much as on the feature itself, so auditing should be tuned rather than maximized.

title: Uba-orl: Unlearning-Activated Backdoor Attacks On Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Fengyi Wang, Cong Li, Lulu Xue, Qiyu Leng, Ziqi Zhou, Peijin Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (offline RL) enables policy learning from pre-collected static datasets without online exploration, and is increasingly deployed not only in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving and robotic control but also in data-mining applications such as recommendation and behavior analysis. While compliance-driven data removal enhances privacy, it also opens a previously unrecognized attack surface. We introduce UBA-ORL (Unlearning-activated Backdoor Attack on Offline Reinforcement Learning), the first unlearning-activated backdoor attack for offline RL: in the evaluated settings, the attack is substantially suppressed after normal training and becomes pronounced after a compliance-driven deletion (unlearning) request. UBA-ORL employs a dual-sample mechanism: alongside backdoor trajectories (BD) that link a trigger to malicious actions under inflated rewards, the attacker injects camouflage trajectories (CM) sharing the same trigger pattern but preserving benign actions with equally high rewards. During training, BD and CM provide competing supervisory signals; upon a legitimate deletion request on the CM subset, the residual BD signal can re-dominate, reactivating the backdoor on demand. Empirical results show that UBA-ORL achieves controllable activation under the evaluated offline-RL configurations, while no-trigger return changes vary by configuration, exposing a previously overlooked security risk in compliance-driven offline RL platforms. We urge the community to develop joint pre-/post-unlearning auditing mechanisms for compliant unlearning services.
tldr: The paper introduces UBA-ORL, the first unlearning-activated backdoor attack on offline reinforcement learning, where a backdoor is suppressed by normal training but reactivated after a compliance-driven data deletion request.
motivation: Compliance-driven data removal in offline RL creates a new attack surface: an adversary can hide a backdoor until unlearning removes camouflage data, then reactivate it.
method: UBA-ORL injects backdoor trajectories linking a trigger to malicious actions and camouflage trajectories with the same trigger but benign actions; competing signals suppress the backdoor until deletion of the camouflage subset lets the backdoor signal dominate.
result: Experiments show controllable activation of the backdoor after unlearning under evaluated offline-RL configurations, with no-trigger return changes depending on the configuration.
conclusion: The work exposes a previously overlooked security risk in compliance-driven offline RL and calls for joint pre-/post-unlearning auditing mechanisms.

title: Mate: Policy-Aware Security Auditing For Mobile Agents Via Synthesis-Driven Trajectory Learning
authors: Changyue Jiang, Jiayi Wang, Xin Wen, Jiarun Dai, Geng Hong, Xudong Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile agents powered by foundation models now automate complex, multi-step workflows on real devices, but their trajectories can violate app-specific security policies. Existing trajectory-level defenses rely on LLM prompting or rigid rules, and thus fail to support fine-grained, natural-language policies that generalize across apps and tasks. In this work, we introduce MATE, a lightweight, policy-conditioned auditor that encodes both agent trajectories and natural-language security policies to determine whether a trajectory violates a given policy and to explain why. Treating policies as editable text rather than fixed model parameters allows MATE to handle user-defined and evolving requirements without retraining. To construct MATE, we build a knowledge base by extracting app descriptions, workflows, and policies from hundreds of popular mobile apps worldwide, and synthesizing over 140K semantically realistic, policy-conditioned trajectories with a multi-stage pipeline. We further release MATEBench, a trajectory-level auditing benchmark with two synthetic subsets and one real-world subset of manually collected trajectories. Models trained with our synthesis-driven trajectory learning achieve over 95% accuracy on MATEBench, retain strong performance on external safety benchmarks, and audit trajectories from Zhipu's AutoGLM and Alibaba's Mobile-Agent on real devices with over 95% accuracy, outperforming prior methods by over 20%. MATE shows that practical, fine-grained security auditing for heterogeneous mobile agents is both feasible and effective.
tldr: MATE is a lightweight policy-conditioned auditor for detecting security-policy violations in mobile agent trajectories using synthesis-driven trajectory learning.
motivation: Foundation-model-powered mobile agents can violate app-specific security policies, but existing trajectory-level defenses rely on rigid rules or LLM prompting and cannot handle fine-grained, natural-language policies that generalize across apps and tasks.
method: MATE encodes agent trajectories and natural-language security policies as editable text, and is trained on a knowledge base of app descriptions, workflows, and policies from hundreds of apps, plus over 140K synthesized policy-conditioned trajectories.
result: MATE achieves over 95% accuracy on the released MATEBench and on real-device trajectories from Zhipu AutoGLM and Alibaba Mobile-Agent, outperforming prior methods by over 20%.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that practical, fine-grained security auditing for heterogeneous mobile agents is feasible and effective.

title: The Price Of Safety: Benign-Case Utility And Token Overhead Of Memory-Poisoning Defenses In Llm Agents
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-poisoning defenses for LLM agents are typically evaluated by their ability to prevent attacks. However, the traffic they process is rarely adversarial. The cost of implementing a defense is paid with each interaction, while its benefits are only seen in a small percentage of cases. We developed a measurement setup that keeps the memory backend, retrieval process, and judge consistent across different conditions, changing only the defense itself. We test each condition three times across five conversations to distinguish the defense's real effects from noise inherent in the pipeline's runs, which remains significant even at temperature zero. Across three write-time defenses (input sanitization, provenance checking, and LLM-based anomaly detection) and one read-time defense (reranking), tested on entirely benign traffic, the write-time defenses show no utility cost we can resolve, with 95% confidence intervals spanning roughly +/-4.5 points and including zero. The reranker is different: it lowers core accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [-9.0,-0.05], bootstrap; McNemar p=0.064), a result that survives replication but sits at the edge of our resolution. Its clearer cost is mechanical rather than statistical. On conversations containing no attack, the reranker quarantines legitimate memories on 33.6% of adjudicated items, reaching as many as 106 false quarantines in a single conversation, at 2.7% token overhead. Stacking all four defenses does not compound this cost: the combined condition's accuracy loss is smaller, and its confidence interval includes zero, suggesting the write-time defenses may partly offset what the reranker discards. Where a defense intercepts the pipeline, not whether it uses an LLM, appears to determine its benign-case price.
tldr: This paper measures the benign-case utility and token overhead costs of memory-poisoning defenses in LLM agents, finding that write-time defenses have unresolved utility costs while reranking incurs measurable false quarantine and small token overhead.
motivation: Memory-poisoning defenses for LLM agents are typically evaluated only on adversarial traffic, but real-world traffic is mostly benign, so the cost of deploying such defenses on every interaction may outweigh their occasional benefits.
method: The authors build a controlled measurement setup that holds the memory backend, retrieval process, and judge constant while varying only the defense, testing three write-time defenses and one read-time defense across five conversations with three repetitions per condition on entirely benign traffic.
result: Write-time defenses show no utility cost resolvable above noise (95% CIs spanning roughly ±4.5 points and including zero), while the read-time reranker lowers core accuracy by 4.4 points and quarantines legitimate memories on 33.6% of adjudicated items, reaching up to 106 false quarantines in one conversation at 2.7% token overhead.
conclusion: The benign-case price of a defense appears to be determined mainly by where it intercepts the pipeline rather than whether it uses an LLM, and stacking defenses does not compound the reranker's cost.

title: When Label Noise Meets Class Imbalance: A Robust Framework For Android Malware Family Classification
authors: Haolan Zhang, Cuiying Gao, Fulin Zhao, Heng Li, Haoran Wang, Chang Luo, Tiejun Wu, Hui Shu, Wei Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning methods for Android malware family classification have achieved high accuracy, but their application is hindered by two major challenges. First, the widely used code obfuscation severely disrupts the automated labeling process and introduces substantial label noise into training datasets. Second, training datasets often exhibit severe class imbalance, leading to poor performance of family classification models. Although existing studies have proposed various solutions to either label noise or class imbalance, they often overlook the interplay between these two factors. Under class imbalance, the presence of hard-to-learn minority-class samples can significantly impair the effectiveness of existing countermeasures for noisy samples. To jointly address label noise and class imbalance, we propose a robust Android malware family classification framework, RoMaC. It employs a self-training strategy to correct noisy labels and, more importantly, discriminately treats head-family and tail-family samples. This design effectively mitigates the adverse impact of class imbalance on noise-robust learning. Moreover, RoMaC integrates a class reweighting mechanism with multi-model ensemble learning, thereby enhancing both classification accuracy and noise robustness. We evaluate RoMaC on a combined dataset constructed from two public datasets. When 30% of the samples are obfuscated, RoMaC achieves an overall Macro-F1 score of 0.803 and an accuracy of 0.871, as well as a tail-class Macro-F1 score of 0.672 and an accuracy of 0.784. Compared with existing methods, RoMaC demonstrates performance improvements of 6%-20% across various obfuscation scenarios and noise levels.
tldr: The paper proposes RoMaC, a robust machine learning framework for Android malware family classification that jointly addresses label noise and class imbalance.
motivation: Existing Android malware family classifiers suffer from code obfuscation-induced label noise and severe class imbalance, and prior work treats these two issues separately.
method: RoMaC uses self-training to correct noisy labels, discriminatively handles head and tail families, and combines class reweighting with multi-model ensemble learning.
result: On a combined public dataset with 30% obfuscated samples, RoMaC achieves Macro-F1 0.803, accuracy 0.871, tail-class Macro-F1 0.672, and tail-class accuracy 0.784, outperforming existing methods by 6%-20% across obfuscation and noise scenarios.
conclusion: The framework effectively mitigates the interplay between label noise and class imbalance, improving Android malware family classification robustness and tail-class performance.

title: Wideband Physical Layer Security In Mixed Near-Field And Far-Field Communications
authors: Yunpu Zhang, Changsheng You, Hing Cheung So
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior studies on wideband physical layer security (PLS) have mostly focused on either far-field or near-field communication systems. In this paper, we investigate PLS in a more general and practical mixed near-field and far-field wideband communication scenario, where a base station (BS) equipped with an extremely large-scale array (XL-array) serves multiple legitimate users in the far field, while a near-field eavesdropper attempts to intercept confidential information at close range. Specifically, we formulate an optimization problem to maximize the secrecy rate of all legitimate users across all subcarriers by jointly designing the transmit beamforming and artificial noise (AN), subject to per-subcarrier power constraints. To gain useful insights into the unique characteristics of mixed-field wideband PLS, we first analyze a special case with a single legitimate user and an eavesdropper. Interestingly, we show that the secure transmission regions in mixed-field wideband systems are not the same across all subcarriers, as revealed by subcarrier-specific secrecy conditions derived from the Fresnel integrals. Moreover, we theoretically demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective AN into the system offers two key benefits: 1) it transforms originally insecure subcarriers into secure ones, and 2) it substantially improves the overall secrecy performance. For the general multiuser setup, we propose an efficient two-stage hybrid beamforming algorithm to jointly design the transmit beamforming and AN, ensuring secure transmission under mixed-field conditions. Building on our analytical insights, we further develop an efficient and low-complexity algorithm that designs the AN beamformers by directly aligning them with the eavesdropper's channel, thereby eliminating the need to optimize AN beamformers across all subcarriers.
tldr: This paper studies wideband physical layer security in mixed near-field and far-field communications using beamforming and artificial noise to maximize secrecy rate.
motivation: Prior physical layer security studies mostly consider either far-field or near-field wideband systems separately, leaving mixed near-field/far-field wideband scenarios underexplored.
method: The authors formulate a secrecy rate maximization problem over subcarriers with per-subcarrier power constraints, analyze a single-user case using Fresnel integrals, and propose a two-stage hybrid beamforming plus artificial noise design for multiuser settings.
result: They show that secure transmission regions differ across subcarriers and that frequency-selective artificial noise can turn insecure subcarriers secure and improve overall secrecy performance.
conclusion: The work provides analytical insights and low-complexity algorithms for secure wideband transmission in mixed near-field and far-field communication systems, but it is outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: An Exponential Lower Bound For The Bit Pigeonhole Principle In Resolution Over Parities
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resolution over parities, [MATH], is the characteristic-two version of resolution over linear equations: clauses are disjunctions of affine equations over [MATH]. Superpolynomial size lower bounds were previously known only for restricted refutations: tree-like, regular, or of bounded depth. We prove that every DAG-like [MATH] refutation of the bit pigeonhole principle with [MATH] pigeons and [MATH] holes has more than [MATH] clauses, for every [MATH], with no restriction on regularity or depth. The proof translates an arbitrary refutation with [MATH] clauses into a polynomial calculus refutation of degree [MATH] over [MATH] groups of extension variables in the style of Buss, Impagliazzo, Krajicek, Pudlak, Razborov, and Sgall. One substitution then removes all extension variables at once and leaves a nonzero low-degree polynomial derived from the pigeonhole axioms alone at degree at most [MATH]; a degree lower bound in the style of Razborov, proved through the homology of chessboard complexes, shows that no such derivation exists. The argument also yields a general sufficient condition for [MATH] size lower bounds. The main theorem, this condition, and all their dependencies are formalized in Lean 4, and every statement links to its formal proof. The proof was developed with substantial AI assistance within an open research framework described in the final section.
tldr: The paper proves exponential-size lower bounds for DAG-like resolution-over-parities refutations of the bit pigeonhole principle, using a translation to polynomial calculus over extension variables and a degree lower bound via chessboard-complex homology.
motivation: Lower bounds for resolution over parities were previously known only for restricted refutation classes (tree-like, regular, bounded-depth), leaving the general DAG-like case open.
method: An arbitrary R(lin) refutation with few clauses is translated into a degree-bounded polynomial calculus refutation over groups of extension variables (in the BCKPRS style); a substitution eliminates the extension variables, and a Razborov-style degree lower bound proved via the homology of chessboard complexes rules out the resulting low-degree derivation.
result: Every DAG-like resolution-over-parities refutation of the bit pigeonhole principle with n^2 pigeons and n holes has more than 2^(n^(2-ε)) clauses for every ε > 0, with no regularity or depth restrictions; the argument also yields a general sufficient condition for such size lower bounds, all formalized in Lean 4.
conclusion: The work settles the unrestricted DAG-like case of a longstanding proof-complexity question and is notable for its Lean 4 formalization and AI-assisted development methodology, but it belongs to classical proof/computational complexity and does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: TubeLab: Interactive Inverse Design Of Wind Instrument Bores With Hard Spectral Constraints
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present TubeLab, a browser-based acoustic simulator and inverse design tool for wind instrument bores without tone holes. The direct problem is solved by a Transfer Matrix Method. Inverse design - finding a bore correction that shifts selected resonance frequencies toward specified musical targets - is formulated as a Tikhonov-regularized least-squares problem whose Jacobian is computed by a single adjoint backward pass per mode. Modes whose frequencies must be preserved are handled by a saddle-point formulation that enforces hard equality constraints regardless of the regularization strength. Resonance frequencies agree with state-of-the-art finite-element calculations to within 1.21 cent over eleven geometries and 132 mode pairs. Experimental validation against tap-tone measurements of 16 numerical control-machined didgeridoos spanning six distinct bore designs yields 9.6 cent RMS deviation over 189 matched mode pairs. Replicate specimens of the same nominal bore disagree with each other by 4.5 cent RMS, so about 36% of the residual variance is fabrication scatter.
tldr: TubeLab is a browser-based acoustic simulator and inverse design tool for wind instrument bores, using transfer matrix methods and constrained least-squares optimization.
motivation: The authors aim to enable inverse design of wind instrument bores while enforcing hard constraints on resonance frequencies that must be preserved.
method: The direct problem is solved with a Transfer Matrix Method, and inverse design is formulated as a Tikhonov-regularized least-squares problem with a Jacobian computed via a single adjoint backward pass per mode; hard equality constraints are handled by a saddle-point formulation.
result: Resonance frequencies agree with finite-element calculations to within 1.21 cents over eleven geometries and 132 mode pairs, and experimental validation against 16 machined didgeridoos yields 9.6 cent RMS deviation over 189 matched mode pairs, with about 36% of residual variance attributable to fabrication scatter.
conclusion: TubeLab provides an effective inverse design tool for wind instrument bores with hard spectral constraints, supported by numerical and experimental validation.

title: Ultrafast Light-sheet Optical Tweezers For In Situ Parallelized Biomechanical Characterization Of Cells And Soft Tissues
authors: Krishangi Krishna, Gannon Lemaster, Jieyi Xu, Zhaowei Jiang, Carlonia G. Casas, Zahra Ahmed, Stephanie Roser, Kareen L. K. Coulombe, Anita Shukla, Vikas Srivastava, Kimani C. Toussaint Jr
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative characterization of the mechanical properties of cells and tissues is essential for understanding disease progression and tissue regeneration. Optical tweezers (OT) enable the direct application of biologically relevant forces; however, OT has been limited to single axial indentations of cells, thereby restricting throughput. Furthermore, the use of quadrant photodiodes is insufficient for assessing the large displacements required for biomechanical characterization of tissues. We present light-sheet optical tweezers as a force transducer (LOFT), an approach that improves the throughput by at least 3x through simultaneous multiparticle trapping and parallelized characterization under sub-nN forces. LOFT is achieved by uniquely integrating light-sheet illumination for extended trapping, femtosecond-pulsed lasers to augment the optical gradient force, and videography-based particle tracking for observation of force transduction. The platform is validated through single-cell indentation experiments. We then apply LOFT to myocardial tissue, revealing significant biomechanical differences between healthy and infarcted regions; the interpretation of which is further supported by quantitative multiphoton imaging using the same optical source and platform. This work represents the first demonstration of OT for the mechanical testing of intact soft tissues, and establishes LOFT as a versatile, multifunctional platform for high-throughput, minimally invasive, mechanical characterization of complex biological systems in situ.
