tldr: The paper introduces light-sheet optical tweezers (LOFT) as a force transducer enabling parallelized, high-throughput biomechanical characterization of cells and intact soft tissues.
motivation: Quantitative mechanical characterization of cells and tissues is important for understanding disease progression and tissue regeneration, but conventional optical tweezers are limited to single axial indentations, restricting throughput and precluding tissue-scale measurements.
method: LOFT integrates light-sheet illumination for extended trapping, femtosecond-pulsed lasers to augment the optical gradient force, and videography-based particle tracking for force transduction, validated via single-cell indentation and applied to myocardial tissue.
result: The platform achieves at least 3x improved throughput under sub-nN forces and reveals significant biomechanical differences between healthy and infarcted myocardial regions, corroborated by multiphoton imaging on the same optical platform.
conclusion: This is the first demonstration of optical tweezers for mechanical testing of intact soft tissues, establishing LOFT as a versatile, minimally invasive, high-throughput platform for biomechanical characterization of complex biological systems in situ.

title: Slow Context, Fast Symptoms: Multiscale Temporal Dynamics And Context-Induced Coupling In Psychological Systems
authors: Kyuri Park, Denny Borsboom, Mike H. Lees, Lourens J. Waldorp, Johan Bollen, V\'itor V. Vasconcelos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Psychological dynamics unfold across multiple timescales: symptoms and other psychological states can change rapidly, whereas social, environmental, biological, and developmental conditions often evolve more slowly. We formulate this structure as a stochastic slow-fast system in which binary symptom states form a fast interacting network embedded within a slow contextual field. Pairwise symptom coupling governs interactions within the fast layer, while the contextual field shifts symptom-specific activation tendencies and can itself receive feedback from sustained symptom activation. Simulations show that changes in the slow field can shift the macroscopic activation state of the symptom system even when the underlying interaction matrix remains fixed. Perturbations to the field generate transient increases in symptom activation followed by recovery, while feedback between the fast and slow layers delays recovery and, when sufficiently strong, produces dependence on initial conditions. We further show that when between-person variation in the contextual field is omitted from network estimation, the inferred system exhibits stronger total coupling and nonzero couplings between symptom pairs that are uncoupled in the data-generating model. Thus, slowly varying context can alter both the dynamics and the apparent interaction structure of a fast psychological system. The framework connects psychological network models with slow-fast dynamical systems and provides a formal basis for distinguishing changes in activation from changes in coupling.
tldr: A stochastic slow-fast dynamical systems framework models psychological symptoms as a fast interacting binary network embedded in a slowly varying contextual field, showing how context alters both dynamics and inferred coupling structure.
motivation: Psychological dynamics span multiple timescales, with rapidly changing symptoms and slowly evolving social, environmental, and biological conditions, yet existing network models of psychopathology typically treat these layers as a single stationary system.
method: The authors formulate a stochastic slow-fast system in which binary symptom states form a fast pairwise-interacting network coupled to a slow contextual field that shifts activation tendencies and can receive feedback from sustained symptom activation, analyzed via simulations and network estimation experiments.
result: Slow-field changes shift macroscopic activation even with a fixed interaction matrix; feedback delays recovery and can induce initial-condition dependence, and omitting between-person context variation inflates inferred total coupling and creates spurious symptom couplings.
conclusion: The framework connects psychological network models with slow-fast dynamical systems, offering a formal basis to distinguish changes in activation from genuine changes in coupling.

title: Modifications Of The Continuous Gromov--Hausdorff Distance
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work studies modifications of the Gromov--Hausdorff distance in which the infimum is taken over pairs of morphisms of a given class [MATH] --- the class of morphisms of a subcategory of the category of metric spaces (the [MATH]-Gromov--Hausdorff distance). We prove that the [MATH]-distance depends Lipschitz-continuously on the class [MATH] in the Hausdorff metric on morphisms. As a consequence, for second countable [MATH]-manifolds equipped with a metric compatible with the topology, the smooth distance coincides with the continuous one: [MATH]. We also introduce the partially continuous and partially locally constant distances (continuity is weakened to continuity on an open subset of the support of full measure) and prove that on the class of metric spaces they coincide with the classical Gromov--Hausdorff distance.
tldr: The paper studies variants of the Gromov–Hausdorff distance defined via infima over morphisms of a given class, proving Lipschitz continuity in the class and showing smooth and continuous distances coincide for second-countable manifolds.
motivation: The classical Gromov–Hausdorff distance is a fundamental tool in metric geometry, but restricting the admissible morphisms may yield useful refined metrics for comparing metric spaces and manifolds.
method: The authors define the C-Gromov–Hausdorff distance for a class C of morphisms in a subcategory of metric spaces, prove Lipschitz continuity of the distance with respect to the Hausdorff metric on classes of morphisms, and introduce partially continuous and partially locally constant variants.
result: It is shown that the C-distance depends Lipschitz-continuously on C, that smooth and continuous distances coincide for second-countable manifolds with compatible metrics, and that the partially continuous/locally constant distances reduce to the classical Gromov–Hausdorff distance on metric spaces.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for modified Gromov–Hausdorff distances, with continuity properties that connect smooth and topological notions of distance between manifolds.

title: A Lorentz Endpoint And Quantitative Obstruction For A Cowling-Price Moment Reduction
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $[MATH][MATH]p'=p/(p-1)[MATH]\omega_d=|B(0,1)|[MATH][MATH][MATH]r>d(p-1)[MATH][r-d(p-1)]^{-1/p'}[MATH]1\le |x|\le R[MATH](d\omega_d\log R)^{1/p'}[MATH]L^{1,p}[MATH][MATH][MATH]L^p[MATH]L^{p,1}[MATH][MATH][MATH]q$ reduction. They do not obstruct auxiliary-norm versions of the Wigderson framework, which reach the Cowling--Price range by a different route.
tldr: The paper establishes a Lorentz-type endpoint estimate and a quantitative obstruction for a Cowling–Price moment reduction in the context of $L^{1,p}$ and Lorentz space interpolation, while noting that auxiliary-norm variants of the Wigderson framework remain unobstructed.
motivation: The work appears to be motivated by understanding whether certain moment-reduction arguments used in the Wigderson framework admit endpoint estimates in Lorentz spaces, and where obstructions arise.
method: The author derives endpoint inequalities involving $L^{1,p}$, $L^p$, and $L^{p,1}$ norms over annuli $1\le |x|\le R$, with explicit constants depending on $d$, $p$, and $\log R$.
result: A Lorentz endpoint bound is proved along with a quantitative obstruction showing that the natural moment-reduction route fails, though auxiliary-norm approaches still reach the Cowling–Price range.
conclusion: The paper clarifies the limits of a specific $L^{1,p}$-based reduction technique, showing the obstruction is intrinsic to that route rather than to the broader Cowling–Price problem.

title: Conformal Spherical Splines For The Laplace--Beltrami Operator On Genus-Zero Surfaces: Construction, Algorithm, And Experiments
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every smooth closed Riemannian surface of genus zero is isometric to the unit sphere carrying a conformal metric, the round metric multiplied by a positive factor. This paper solves the Poisson equation and the eigenvalue problem of the Laplace--Beltrami operator of such a metric with smooth spherical splines, taking the conformal factor as the only description of the geometry. Because the Dirichlet energy is conformally invariant in two dimensions, the stiffness matrix is the round-sphere matrix for every conformal metric, and the factor enters only the load vector, the mean-value constraint and the weighted mass matrix. A surface embedded in space with a conformal parametrization, a surface of revolution, and a surface given only as a triangle mesh are instances of the same problem that differ in how the factor is obtained; the first two are treated here, and the factor is checked against an area identity before any equation is discretized. The unknown is a spline on a fixed spherical triangulation in broken Bernstein--B\'ezier form, with [MATH] smoothness imposed algebraically through edge functionals and the conforming space realized by a null-space matrix computed once and reused for every metric. Each step of the computation is stated with the formulas it needs. Experiments on the round metric, a prolate spheroid, a dumbbell of revolution, an Evans--Fung red-blood-cell profile and a prescribed factor with no embedding show the rates [MATH] in [MATH] and [MATH] in energy for spline degree [MATH], the rate [MATH] for eigenvalues with reproduction of the even-order eigenvalues of the round metric up to degree [MATH] to roundoff, and, against parametric surface finite elements on the same triangulations, smaller errors at comparable numbers of unknowns for degrees four and six.
tldr: This paper develops conformal spherical splines for solving Poisson and eigenvalue problems of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on genus-zero surfaces.
motivation: Many applications require solving PDEs on curved surfaces, and genus-zero surfaces admit conformal parametrization by the sphere, which can simplify numerical treatment.
method: The authors use smooth spherical splines in broken Bernstein-Bezier form on a fixed spherical triangulation, exploiting conformal invariance of the Dirichlet energy so that the stiffness matrix is the round-sphere matrix, with the conformal factor entering only the load vector and mass matrix.
result: Experiments on various surfaces show optimal convergence rates for spline degrees, eigenvalue accuracy, and smaller errors compared to parametric surface finite elements at comparable numbers of unknowns.
conclusion: The approach provides an efficient and accurate spline-based framework for PDEs on conformal genus-zero surfaces, with potential for extension to mesh-based geometries.

title: Transforming Mathematics
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I believe that the development of AI tools will lead to a transformation of mathematics, both professionally and culturally. However, it will be a tragic missed opportunity if the massive shifts in culture and practice that are underway are motivated and influenced solely by AI. We must aspire to more than this. We can and should collaboratively strive for a future where our cultures, practices, and values are grounded first and foremost in empathy, compassion, justice, and humanity. In this article, I call to action every member of the mathematical community, whether you view yourself as a researcher, teacher, scholar, student, professional, hobbyist, or a combination of these and more.
tldr: A call-to-action essay arguing that the AI-driven transformation of mathematics should be guided by humanistic values such as empathy, compassion, and justice rather than by AI capabilities alone.
motivation: The author believes AI tools will fundamentally reshape the professional and cultural practice of mathematics, and worries this shift will be a tragic missed opportunity if motivated solely by technological momentum.
method: Position paper / commentary offering a normative argument and an appeal to the mathematical community, rather than any formal or empirical methodology.
result: No technical results are presented; the contribution is a set of value-based recommendations and an invitation for community-wide deliberation.
conclusion: The mathematical community should collaboratively pursue a future in which its cultures, practices, and values are grounded first in empathy, compassion, justice, and humanity.

title: Joint Observer-Based Output-Feedback Robust Guidance And Control Funnel Synthesis
authors: Cheng Chang, Shiva Shakeri, Mehran Mesbahi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A joint guidance and robust observer-based output-feedback synthesis framework is developed for discrete-time nonlinear systems subject to bounded process disturbances and measurement noise. The method co-designs a reference trajectory, time-varying Luenberger observer and observer-based linear output-feedback gains, and coupled ellipsoidal funnels that certify conditioned-invariant bounds on tracking and estimation errors. Nonlinear residuals are bounded by incremental quadratic constraints (QCs) parameterized by local Lipschitz constants, estimated via sampling approaches. The coupled stability conditions are formulated as linear matrix inequality (LMI) surrogates and solved using sequential convex programming with proximal regularization (prox-SCP) via semidefinite programming (SDP). Simulations of a unicycle model under persistent sensory noise and system disturbances demonstrate robust tracking and funnel-certified constraint satisfaction with respect to the jointly designed reference trajectory.
tldr: The paper develops a joint guidance-and-control synthesis framework that co-designs a reference trajectory, a time-varying Luenberger observer, output-feedback gains, and coupled ellipsoidal funnels certified via LMIs solved by proximal sequential convex programming.
motivation: Robust tracking under bounded process disturbances and measurement noise requires jointly accounting for estimation and tracking errors, which most separated guidance/control designs do not handle coherently.
method: Nonlinear residuals are bounded using incremental quadratic constraints parameterized by local Lipschitz constants estimated by sampling; coupled stability conditions are relaxed to LMI surrogates and solved with prox-SCP via SDP.
result: Simulations on a unicycle model with persistent sensor noise and disturbances show robust tracking with funnel-certified constraint satisfaction relative to the jointly designed reference trajectory.
conclusion: The approach offers a tractable convex-programming route to certified robust guidance and observer-based output-feedback control for discrete-time nonlinear systems.

title: Efficient Rigorous Continuation Via Chebyshev Series Expansion I
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the global continuation of solution manifolds arising in dynamical systems. We present a rigorous continuation method based on a Chebyshev series expansion of the solution manifold. The branch is first approximated by a high-order Chebyshev interpolation polynomial, and an explicit error bound is then obtained by verifying the contraction of a quasi-Newton operator near this approximation. The contraction is formulated on a weighted [MATH] space, giving a finer control than the typical [MATH]-error bound obtained from the uniform contraction theorem. In fact, the latter follows directly from our contraction operator. Furthermore, we discuss how our strategy applies naturally to pseudo-arclength continuation, where the continuation parameter fails to provide a valid local coordinate, and extends to multi-parameter continuation. Lastly, we detail two applications in which we compute a two-parameter family of steady-states for the Cahn--Hilliard equation, and a one-parameter family of steady-states undergoing saddle-node bifurcations for the Shigesada--Kawasaki--Teramoto system.
tldr: The paper develops a rigorous numerical continuation method for solution manifolds of dynamical systems using high-order Chebyshev series expansions with explicit error bounds from quasi-Newton contraction in a weighted space.
motivation: Classical rigorous continuation schemes rely on uniform contraction theorems that yield coarse uniform error bounds, limiting their effectiveness for stiff or multi-parameter problems.
method: The solution branch is approximated by a high-order Chebyshev interpolation polynomial, and an explicit error bound is derived by verifying contraction of a quasi-Newton operator in a weighted space, extended to pseudo-arclength and multi-parameter continuation.
result: The approach gives finer control than standard uniform error bounds (which follow as a corollary), and is demonstrated on a two-parameter family of Cahn-Hilliard steady states and a saddle-node bifurcation family in the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system.
conclusion: Chebyshev-based rigorous continuation provides a practical and tighter framework for validating solution manifolds in bifurcation problems, though the work lies entirely in numerical analysis rather than quantum information science.

title: From Capability To Assurance In Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: A Framework And Reference Implementation
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Research on large language model agents for penetration testing is evaluated almost entirely by capability: whether the agent captures a flag or reproduces a proof of concept. That metric suits a benchmark but is silent on the properties that decide whether an autonomous agent can be used in an authorized engagement: whether a reported finding is true, whether the agent stayed inside its authorized scope, and whether an operator can audit what it did. We call these assurance properties and argue that they belong to the harness, the runtime wrapping the model, and can be enforced in code. This paper makes three contributions. First, we define a framework of five assurance properties (evidence grounding, non destructive claim reduction, computed severity, enforced authorization, and tamper evident accountability), each with a formal model and an explicit acceptance test, connected to prior work in capability based security, tamper evident logging, and software provenance. Second, we position representative systems (PentestGPT, the Cochise reference harness, MAPTA, and the trajectory judge PentestJudge) within the framework using published coding criteria, and identify a consistent assurance gap. Third, we study one open source implementation, NeuroSploit, pinned to an exact commit, reporting its architecture, its complexity cost, and a content addressed artifact bundle from a run against a public deliberately vulnerable target. We execute the deterministic authorization and audit acceptance tests directly and find and report a real enforcement gap, which we reflect by scoring both properties as partial. We therefore claim an initial existence argument that the properties are realizable together, not a comparative performance result, and we specify the multi target, ablation, and adversarial evaluation protocol required to turn the framework obligations into measurements.
tldr: The paper proposes a framework of five 'assurance properties' for autonomous LLM-based penetration-testing harnesses and evaluates one open-source implementation against it.
motivation: Research on LLM agents for penetration testing is evaluated almost solely by capability (capturing flags, reproducing PoCs), which says nothing about whether findings are truthful, whether the agent stayed in scope, or whether its actions can be audited.
method: The authors define five assurance properties (evidence grounding, non-destructive claim reduction, computed severity, enforced authorization, tamper-evident accountability) each with a formal model and acceptance test, position existing systems (PentestGPT, Cochise, MAPTA, PentestJudge) within this framework, and analyze the NeuroSploit implementation pinned to a specific commit against a deliberately vulnerable target.
result: The framework reveals a consistent assurance gap across existing systems, and executing the deterministic authorization and audit acceptance tests against NeuroSploit exposed a real enforcement gap, scored as partial on both properties.
conclusion: The work provides an initial existence argument that the assurance properties are realizable together rather than a comparative performance result, and specifies a multi-target, ablation, and adversarial evaluation protocol needed to convert these obligations into measurements.

title: A Horizon-Independent Regret Bound For Optimistic Hedge In General-Sum Games
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can simple learning rules keep their regret bounded in self-play? Recent work achieves constant regret bounds through modified regularization and higher-order prediction. Yet for Optimistic Hedge, arguably the most canonical method in games, the best known individual regret bound remains logarithmic. In this work, we prove that plain Optimistic Hedge with a constant step size can attain [MATH] individual regret in general-sum games with [MATH] players and [MATH] actions, under expected loss-vector feedback. As a corollary, its time-averaged play enjoys an [MATH] coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) gap. Our analysis represents Optimistic Hedge as a real-analytic recurrence on a compact space, which yields an exact finite-order difference relation that eliminates horizon dependence. Our proof hinges on nonconstructive Noetherianity argument of Frisch (1967), so the [MATH]-dependence remains implicit.
tldr: This paper proves a horizon-independent individual regret bound for plain Optimistic Hedge in general-sum games using a real-analytic recurrence and a nonconstructive Noetherianity argument.
motivation: The best known individual regret bound for Optimistic Hedge, a canonical game-theoretic learning rule, was only logarithmic, while recent modified methods achieve constant regret. The paper asks whether plain Optimistic Hedge can also attain horizon-independent regret.
method: The authors represent Optimistic Hedge as a real-analytic recurrence on a compact space, derive an exact finite-order difference relation that eliminates horizon dependence, and use Frisch's nonconstructive Noetherianity argument to obtain the bound.
result: Under expected loss-vector feedback, plain Optimistic Hedge with constant step size achieves individual regret polynomial in the number of players and actions, independent of the time horizon, and consequently its time-averaged play has a coarse correlated equilibrium gap of the same order.
conclusion: The work shows that the canonical Optimistic Hedge can achieve horizon-independent regret in general-sum games, though the bound's dependence on the number of actions remains implicit due to the nonconstructive proof technique.

title: When Agentic Trust Crosses Organizational Boundaries: Structural Externalization And A Reference Model For Trust Evidence
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems increasingly invoke tools, services, data, and other agents across organizational boundaries, yet a relying party cannot assess a delegated action solely from producing-domain controls and records. This paper develops Trustworthiness as a Service (TaaS) through a synthesis of trustworthy-AI governance, agent security, distributed trust management, identity, provenance, assurance, and control-plane research. The analytical unit is a cross-domain reliance proposition that names the issuer, subject and action, relying party, administrative boundary, evidence dependencies, adverse condition, and required verification or adjudication semantics. The three-condition structural-externalization diagnostic identifies propositions that depend on multiple domains, require producer-independent reliance, and must remain reviewable after revocation, failure, conflicting records, or dispute. For such propositions, the paper specifies a trust-evidence envelope: an immutable workflow manifest linked to append-only, issuer-attributed attestations for task-scoped authority, policy and execution decisions, provenance, validity, disclosure, status, challenge, and recovery. A topology-neutral logical reference model assigns these functions to explicit roles and trust domains. Three analytical scenarios and the TaaS-Eval protocol proposal define manifests, independent consumers, hard gates, adversarial evidence tests, metrics, and reproducible artifact reporting. By composing established identity, authorization, provenance, assurance, and governance mechanisms around a bounded delegated action, TaaS provides a reusable profile for cross-domain reliance. It makes evidence dependencies, independent verification, challenge, and recovery explicit, supporting interoperable governance and future evaluation without treating producer assertions as ground truth.
tldr: The paper proposes 'Trustworthiness as a Service' (TaaS), a reference model and evidence-envelope architecture for assessing trust when autonomous agents delegate actions across organizational boundaries.
motivation: Agentic AI systems increasingly invoke tools, services, and other agents across administrative domains, but a relying party cannot verify a delegated action using only the producing domain's controls and records.
method: The authors synthesize literature on trustworthy-AI governance, agent security, distributed trust management, identity, provenance, and assurance to define a cross-domain reliance proposition and a three-condition structural-externalization diagnostic, then specify a trust-evidence envelope of append-only issuer-attributed attestations and a topology-neutral logical reference model.
result: Three analytical scenarios and the proposed TaaS-Eval protocol illustrate manifests, independent consumers, hard gates, adversarial evidence tests, and metrics for reproducible evaluation of cross-domain reliance.
conclusion: TaaS offers a reusable governance profile that makes evidence dependencies, independent verification, challenge, and recovery explicit, supporting interoperable evaluation without treating producer assertions as ground truth.

title: Secrets That Survive Everything: Runtime Credential Exposure In Production Web Applications
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-deployment secret scanning operates only on source code, never on what a production application serves. We document two exploitation chains in which Azure AD client credentials and APIM subscription keys from production JavaScript bundles enabled account takeover and mass data exposure. An authorized engagement covered approximately 2,000 enterprise web assets in one organization; 113 (5.65%) served live credentials. To quantify the shift-right gap, we built an independent Ground Truth (GT-194) of 194 secret-grade credentials through Claude Opus 4.7 extraction and manual analyst review, with the 247 LLM-extracted candidates independently validated by GPT-5.5 (Brennan-Prediger kappa = 0.676). The principal finding is structural: 13.9% of GT-194 (27 of 194) is surfaced only by manual analysis and recovered by none of the nine evaluated production scanners, a tool-agnostic blind spot the ground-truth model also misses. CryptoJS encrypted configuration separately defeats every static scanner: the credential exists only after decryption with a co-located key, reached only by runtime-aware detection. Combined coverage plateaus at 86.1%. Among the nine scanners, the best static scanner recovers 36.6% and the best runtime-aware scanner 77.8% (F1 = 0.818, McNemar p < 0.001); the ground-truth model is reported separately as a reference comparator, not an evaluated detector. On 63 of 86 secret-exposed applications (73.3%), the full Azure AD token-mint chain is co-located in one bundle, reachable from browser code. We characterize five paths by which credentials reach production undetected and present a layered runtime detection methodology and remediation framework. Recall is scoped to a single-organization Azure-heavy corpus.
tldr: The paper documents runtime credential exposure in production web applications and evaluates detection tools for secrets in JavaScript bundles.
motivation: Pre-deployment secret scanning only checks source code, leaving a gap for credentials exposed in production JavaScript, which can enable account takeover and data exposure.
method: An authorized engagement analyzed approximately 2,000 enterprise web assets in one organization, using Claude Opus 4.7 extraction, manual analyst review, GPT-5.5 validation, and nine production scanners to quantify detection blind spots.
result: 113 of 2,000 assets served live credentials; 13.9% of the ground-truth credentials were found only manually and missed by all nine scanners, with combined coverage plateauing at 86.1%.
conclusion: Runtime-aware detection and a layered remediation framework are needed to close the shift-right gap for secrets that become exposed only at application runtime.

title: SoK: From Finding To Deployment: Systematizing The Os Kernel Bug Lifecycle
authors: Luyao Bai, Gengda She, Kenan Alghythee, Hang Zhang, Xiaoguang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated kernel bug discovery has advanced rapidly. Continuous fuzzing and static analysis systems, such as syzbot, now expose Linux kernel bugs at a scale that downstream processes struggle to absorb. Yet a crash report is only the beginning. Before a bug is eliminated, it must be triaged, understood, patched, validated, reviewed, integrated, and often backported. These later stages remain far less automated, creating a persistent gap between bug discovery and patch deployment. This SoK systematizes the Linux kernel bug lifecycle from discovery to deployment. We organize prior work and production systems into five stages: discovery, triage, patch generation, patch validation, and integration. We explain the resulting automation gradient through kernel-specific challenges such as concurrency, implicit invariants, cross-syscall state, hardware dependence, lack of fault isolation, and architecture/configuration multiplicity. We further ground the analysis in a measurement of real syzbot-fixed bugs. The data shows that the crash-to-patch gap is not merely a backlog of unfixed reports but a structural failure mode of the repair pipeline: even after being fixed, bugs often remain open for weeks, require review-driven patch revisions, or lack reproducers that current repair and validation systems assume. This exposes a mismatch between where kernel-security automation is mature and where bug closure actually breaks down. These findings expose a deeper mismatch: today's repair and validation techniques often assume reliable reproducers, localized root causes, and checkable correctness oracles, yet these are precisely the artifacts missing from many real kernel bug reports. Closing the crash-to-patch gap, therefore, requires treating such artifacts as outputs to be produced, not prerequisites to be assumed.
tldr: This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper organizes the Linux kernel bug lifecycle into five stages—discovery, triage, patch generation, patch validation, and integration—and characterizes the persistent automation gap between crash discovery and patch deployment.
motivation: Automated kernel bug discovery via continuous fuzzing and static analysis (e.g., syzbot) has outpaced downstream repair processes, leaving a structural 'crash-to-patch' gap that prior work has not systematically characterized.
method: The authors systematize prior work and production systems across five lifecycle stages and ground the analysis in a measurement study of real syzbot-fixed bugs, analyzing fix latency, review-driven revisions, and missing reproducers.
result: The measurement shows the crash-to-patch gap is not merely a backlog: even after fixing, bugs often stay open for weeks, require review-driven patch revisions, or lack the reproducers that repair and validation tools assume.
conclusion: Closing the gap requires treating artifacts such as reliable reproducers, localized root causes, and checkable correctness oracles as outputs to be produced rather than prerequisites to be assumed, motivating a rethinking of kernel-security automation.

title: Coven-Meyerowitz T2 Necessity Through Coprime Stripe Collapse
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every finite subset of the integers which tiles by translations satisfies the Coven-Meyerowitz condition T2, with no restriction on the number of prime factors or their exponents. Together with the necessity of T1 and the sufficiency of T1 and T2 proved by Coven and Meyerowitz, this gives their proposed characterization of finite integer tiles. The proof uses strong induction on a cyclic tiling period. Character identities produce periodic Boolean product stripes; integral descent to a coprime quotient and the Frobenius identity force a common orientation. Independent phase shifts then give smaller-period tilings from which the mixed cyclotomic zeros of the original factors can be recovered. A companion Lean formalization verifies the unrestricted T2 necessity statement.
tldr: The paper proves the Coven-Meyerowitz T2 necessity for all finite integer tiles using coprime stripe collapse and a Lean formalization, completing their proposed characterization.
motivation: The Coven-Meyerowitz conjectures are central to the theory of finite integer tiling, and the unrestricted necessity of T2 had remained open.
method: The proof uses strong induction on a cyclic tiling period, periodic Boolean product stripes, integral descent to a coprime quotient, and the Frobenius identity to force a common orientation.
result: Every finite integer tile satisfies T2 without restrictions on prime factors or exponents, yielding the full Coven-Meyerowitz characterization when combined with known T1 necessity and T1+T2 sufficiency.
conclusion: The work resolves the unrestricted T2 necessity and supports the theorem with a companion Lean formal verification.

title: At Least One Of The Three Numbers $\zeta(5)$, $\zeta(7)$, $\zeta(9)$ Is Irrational
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we prove the irrationality of at least one of the three numbers [MATH] and [MATH] is irrational. We find linear forms in [MATH] and [MATH] and prove their arithmetic by Kranttenthaler and Rivoal. We also refine these estimates by using integral quantity [MATH] involving specific product of prime powers. We use the results of Kranttenthaler, Rivoal and Zudilin to prove that at least one of the three numbers [MATH] and [MATH] is irrational.
tldr: The paper proves that at least one of the Riemann zeta values ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9) is irrational using linear forms and arithmetic estimates.
motivation: Irrationality results for odd zeta values beyond ζ(3) remain largely open, and the authors aim to extend known partial results to the trio ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9).
method: The authors construct linear forms in zeta values following Krantzenthaler and Rivoal, refine them using an integral quantity involving products of prime powers, and invoke results of Krantzenthaler, Rivoal, and Zudilin.
result: They establish that at least one of ζ(5), ζ(7), ζ(9) is irrational, improving on previous estimates through refined arithmetic bounds.
conclusion: The work advances the classical problem of the irrationality of odd zeta values, but it lies entirely within analytic number theory and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Discovering Heron's Triangle Area Formula In A Morning In The Rain
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivations and derivations for Heron's triangle area formula abound. But how would one the formula? We recount the challenge of designing a laboratory experiment to discover Heron's formula, and of doing so in the morning, in time for a noon class---a snapshot of collaboration with AI in fall 2025. We then reflect on extensions and generalizations.
tldr: A narrative account of designing a laboratory experiment to discover Heron's triangle area formula with AI collaboration.
motivation: To explore how one might discover Heron's formula through experimentation and collaboration with AI, and to reflect on extensions and generalizations.
method: Recounts the challenge of designing a laboratory experiment to derive Heron's formula in a short time frame, in time for a noon class.
result: The paper describes the process and reflections but presents no quantum information theory or related physical results.
conclusion: The work is unrelated to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Criterion For Classifying Elliptic Curve That Are Unsolvable In The Set Integers
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we establish a criterion for classifying elliptic curves that have no solutions in the set of positive integers. In particular, we prove that if [MATH] is an elliptic curve where [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] are coefficients of the curve, and [MATH] is a prime number where [MATH], and [MATH] is a positive integer point, then if $[MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH][MATH]E[MATH]E(^{+}) = \varnothing$. Specifically, we introduce a matrix construction to establish the nonexistence of positive integer solutions for a family of elliptic curves.
tldr: The paper establishes a criterion for classifying elliptic curves that admit no solutions in the positive integers, using a matrix construction to prove nonexistence of integer points for a family of curves.
motivation: Determining which elliptic curves lack positive integer solutions is a classical problem in number theory, related to Diophantine analysis and the arithmetic of elliptic curves.
method: The author derives a condition on the coefficients and a prime divisor of an elliptic curve such that no positive integer point exists, and generalizes this via a linear-algebraic matrix construction.

conclusion: The work provides a number-theoretic classification tool for elliptic curves without positive integer solutions, with no apparent connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Combinatorial Problem In Cinema Seating
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We address a problem concerning cinema audiences: ``A cinema has [MATH] seats numbered from [MATH] to [MATH], and there are [MATH] people with tickets numbered from [MATH] to [MATH]. People enter the cinema in order. If someone has the ticket number [MATH], they can choose seats whose numbers are multiples of [MATH]. They should exit the cinema if the permitted seats are occupied by previous audience members. In how many ways can they be seated under these conditions?" We give an algorithm to create the list of situations that meet these conditions. We also focus on finding the number of situations in two special cases: when exactly one seat is unoccupied whose total number is denoted by [MATH], and when all audiences [MATH] are seated, whose total number is denoted by [MATH]. Giving the recursive formula [MATH] with the initial value [MATH], we provide an explicit formula for [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] are distinct prime numbers. Furthermore, we show that [MATH].

motivation: The authors aim to solve a recreational-style combinatorial problem involving ticket numbers, seat multiples, and exit conditions.
method: They provide an algorithm to generate valid seating situations and derive recursive and explicit formulas for special cases.
result: They obtain a recursive formula and an explicit formula for cases involving distinct prime numbers, including exact counts for one unoccupied seat and full seating.
conclusion: The work is a pure combinatorics contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Interval Number For Tournaments In P3-convexity
authors: Idian C. Capozzoli, Yan S. Couto, Enrique Junchaya

For each [MATH], we show that determining whether [MATH] is W[2]-complete when parameterized by [MATH]. Moreover, under ETH, we show that there is no parameterized algorithm for that problem with running time [MATH] on an [MATH]-vertex tournament, where [MATH] is any computable function. For the [MATH]-convexity, we also show that [MATH], which yields a simple quasi-polynomial [MATH] brute-force algorithm. On the other hand, under ETH, we show that the problem is NP-intermediate, that is, it is neither NP-hard nor in P. For the [MATH]-convexity, the same brute force algorithm is not quasi-polynomial, since we present a family of instances with [MATH]. We conjecture that this problem is NP-complete.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of computing interval numbers of tournaments under P3-convexity and a related convexity, establishing W[2]-completeness and ETH-based hardness results.
motivation: Interval numbers in graph convexities generalize classical graph parameters, and understanding their complexity in tournament graphs clarifies the boundary between tractable and intractable cases.
method: The authors analyze parameterized and exact complexity of determining interval numbers in two convexity structures on tournaments, proving W[2]-completeness, ETH-conditional running-time lower bounds, and a quasi-polynomial brute-force algorithm for one of the convexities.

conclusion: Tournament interval numbers exhibit rich and subtle complexity behavior across convexities, with strong hardness evidence and an open conjecture for the remaining case.

title: SelfOp: An Optimization Algorithm For Self-Improving Security Agents
authors: Saad Ullah, Yigitcan Kaya, Christopher Kruegel, Giovanni Vigna, Gianluca Stringhini
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for security tasks: vulnerability discovery, exploit reproduction, and patch generation. Improving them at the model level demands expert demonstrations or computable rewards, which security tasks rarely offer: traces are costly, failures hard to diagnose, rewards sparse, and non-computable. Efforts thus shift to the harness and context, but manual tuning needs task-specific expertise and scales poorly, while automated methods rely on scarce ground truth, stronger optimizer models, or unguided propose-and-evaluate loops that reduce to costly trial and error. We introduce SelfOp, an algorithm that automatically improves a frozen security agent's task context (instructions, skills, and reference documents), without modifying its execution harness and model weights. SelfOp casts context optimization as chain-rule-inspired textual gradient descent: from a single instance's outcome, it propagates error signals backward through the evaluator, the agent's trajectory, and the context artifacts that shaped its behavior, yielding per-instance textual gradients. Gradients are accumulated across instances by clustering, ranking, and filtering, and committed only under cross-instance consensus. A convergence detector monitors the gradient signal itself and stops once the context has absorbed the generalizable information in the training data, without held-out validation data. We evaluate SelfOp on CyberGym, a benchmark of real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks. With fewer than 200 training examples, SelfOp yields a 17-point self-improvement for GPT-5.4-mini (with Codex), enough to surpass the frontier GPT-5.4 baseline by 6 points, and an 18.5-point self-improvement for GPT-5.4 itself. The optimized skills also transfer across models, highlighting that SelfOp-optimized skills learn generalizable task knowledge not model-specific patterns.
tldr: SelfOp is a textual-gradient-descent algorithm that automatically improves the task context of a frozen LLM security agent without changing its harness or model weights.
motivation: LLM agents for security tasks are hard to improve at the model level due to costly traces, sparse non-computable rewards, and limited expert demonstrations, while manual context tuning scales poorly.
method: SelfOp treats context optimization as chain-rule-inspired textual gradient descent, propagating error signals from an instance outcome backward through evaluator, agent trajectory, and context artifacts, then accumulating gradients via clustering/ranking/filtering and committing under cross-instance consensus.
result: On CyberGym vulnerability reproduction, SelfOp improves GPT-5.4-mini with Codex by 17 points and GPT-5.4 by 18.5 points using fewer than 200 training examples, with optimized skills transferring across models.
conclusion: Automated textual-gradient context optimization can yield generalizable self-improvement in frozen LLM security agents without held-out validation or harness modifications.

title: SMS-delivered Network-initiated Supl On Pixel 8: A Privacy Assessment
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A SUPL\_INIT message is a network-initiated trigger that can be sent to a handset using an SMS to unilaterally start a location session: on receipt, the handset is instructed to determine its own position and report it, together with an identifier such as its IMSI, to a server specified in the message, without any action by the phone's user. The concern motivating this investigation is whether such a message could be used to silently exfiltrate a handset's location and subscriber identity to a server under an attacker's control. We investigated this on a Google Pixel 8 handset, which uses a Samsung Exynos modem and a Broadcom GPS/GNSS subsystem. We find no privacy issue: the handset never sends location data to an attacker-chosen server as a result of an unsolicited SUPL\_INIT delivered by SMS.
tldr: A privacy assessment of whether an SMS-delivered SUPL_INIT message can silently trigger location exfiltration on a Google Pixel 8 finds no such privacy issue.
motivation: To investigate whether network-initiated SUPL_INIT messages sent via SMS could be abused to silently obtain a handset's location and subscriber identity from an attacker-controlled server.
method: The authors tested an unsolicited SUPL_INIT delivered by SMS on a Google Pixel 8 handset using a Samsung Exynos modem and Broadcom GPS/GNSS subsystem.
result: The handset never sent location data to an attacker-chosen server in response to the unsolicited SUPL_INIT message.
conclusion: The investigated SUPL_INIT attack vector does not pose a privacy risk on the tested Pixel 8 configuration.

title: Beyond Single-Model Injection: A Threat Model And Defense Architecture For Prompt Injection In Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing prompt injection research focuses on single-model chatbot scenarios, where an attacker manipulates one LLM through crafted input. Multi-agent systems amplify this threat through three mechanisms absent from single-model settings: inter-agent message passing creates injection channels invisible to perimeter defenses, shared tool access enables privilege escalation across agent boundaries, and trust propagation allows a compromised agent to influence upstream orchestrators. We construct a threat model enumerating 14 attack vectors across four categories: direct injection via user input (3 vectors), indirect injection via tool outputs (4 vectors), inter-agent injection via message passing (4 vectors), and cascading injection through orchestrator manipulation (3 vectors). Testing all 14 vectors against a 6-agent production-representative system, we find that 67% of agents are vulnerable to at least one scope violation even with system-prompt-level guardrails, and indirect injection via tool outputs succeeds in 43% of attempts. Four architectural defenses reduce overall injection success from 31.2% to 4.2%: message signing with provenance tracking (inter-agent injection down 91%), input/output sanitization at agent boundaries (indirect injection down 78%), privilege-scoped tool access per agent role (privilege escalation eliminated entirely), and anomaly detection on inter-agent communication patterns (84% of cascading attempts caught).
tldr: The paper introduces a threat model for prompt injection in multi-agent LLM systems and evaluates four architectural defenses against 14 attack vectors.
motivation: Existing prompt injection research focuses on single-model chatbots, leaving multi-agent LLM systems—which introduce inter-agent message passing, shared tool access, and trust propagation—understudied.
method: The authors enumerate 14 attack vectors across four categories and test them against a 6-agent production-representative system, then evaluate four defenses: message signing with provenance tracking, input/output sanitization at agent boundaries, privilege-scoped tool access, and anomaly detection on inter-agent communication.
result: 67% of agents are vulnerable to at least one scope violation despite system-prompt guardrails, and indirect injection via tool outputs succeeds in 43% of attempts; the defenses reduce overall injection success from 31.2% to 4.2%.
conclusion: Multi-agent LLM systems require defense-in-depth beyond single-model guardrails, as architectural defenses can substantially mitigate prompt injection risks.

title: Dual-Locking Learned Ai Models: A PIN-Based Sparse Qim Watermarking And Adaptive Index Permutation Approach
authors: Iva Vasic, Jes\'us Mu\~noz-C\'adiz, Bata Vasic
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a dual-locking method for securing trained neural networks that combines key-driven index permutation with PIN-based watermarking based on Sparse Quantization Index Modulation (QIM). Cryptographic randomness is introduced by independently applying a uniform random permutation to each row of adaptively selected index vectors. A robust blind binary watermark is then embedded into the bias coefficients by modulating their quantized values, binding the network to a user-defined Personal Identification Number (PIN). Without the correct key, the network retains its architecture but becomes functionally impaired due to disrupted internal representations. Inverse permutation fully restores the original model accuracy, while the embedded watermark remains imperceptible and enables blind verification of key association and model authorship. To improve both locking effectiveness and recoverability, an adaptive key selection strategy redistributes high-magnitude weights to low-sensitivity positions and vice versa, increasing degradation in the locked state while preserving full recovery. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet-1K using fully connected networks, ResNet CNNs, and transformer architectures show that locking reduces accuracy below 10\%, and even below 0.5\% for CNNs, while the correct key fully restores performance. The watermark introduces no measurable accuracy degradation and reliably authenticates ownership. Analysis of embedding distributions across CNNs and transformers further indicates potential diagnostic value for identifying undertrained or suboptimally designed models. The proposed approach therefore provides simultaneous model protection, recovery, and ownership verification.
tldr: The paper proposes a dual-locking method for protecting trained neural networks using key-driven index permutation and PIN-based sparse quantization index modulation watermarking.
motivation: There is a need to secure trained neural network models against unauthorized use and to verify ownership without degrading performance for legitimate users.
method: The approach combines adaptive cryptographic index permutation with blind watermark embedding into bias coefficients via sparse QIM, binding the model to a user-defined PIN and enabling recovery with the correct key.
result: Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR, and ImageNet with fully connected, ResNet, and transformer models show locked accuracy below 10% (often below 0.5% for CNNs), while the correct key restores full accuracy and the watermark causes no measurable degradation.
conclusion: The method provides simultaneous model protection, recovery, and ownership verification, and may also help diagnose undertrained or suboptimally designed models.

title: Towards Supporting Quantum Grassroots Organizations In Asean
authors: Bethel Loke Hui Ting Amalina Lai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the role of quantum grassroots organizations in The Association of South-east Asian Nations (ASEAN), the challenges they face, and how these organizations can be better supported by other players in the ecosystem of quantum technologies. We look into the goals and strategies of ASEAN grassroots organizations and their potential impacts and investigate the obstacles and challenges currently faced by these groups. We propose providing mentors with specialized knowledge to assist in the refinement of technical content and organizational management, building connections between grassroots and key stakeholders in the quantum space, and creating opportunities to obtain stable funding. These can help to mitigate the aforementioned challenges and ensure its longevity, sustainability, and impact on the wider quantum community.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Weak Values Beyond The Weak Limit: Measurement-Strength Invariance Under Post-Selection
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22976v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weak values are conventionally extracted in the limit of vanishing measurement strength. At finite strength, the corresponding post-selected conditional averages generally acquire nonlinear corrections and need not retain their weak value interpretation. Here we identify a class of measurement protocols for which this expectation fails: the conditional value reconstructed from the measuring probe is exactly independent of the probe strength and therefore coincides with the real part of the weak value. We first analyze this phenomenon in the measurement--disturbance protocol introduced by Lund and Wiseman. We then establish conditions under which this invariance persists, showing that it is determined by the interplay between the probe interaction, a subsequent measurement interaction with an ancillary apparatus, and the final post-selection. These results demonstrate that weak coupling, although generally sufficient for accessing weak values, is not always necessary.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Mathematical Folklore
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present reflections on an experimental seminar studying the human and cultural roots of modern mathematics.
tldr: A reflection on an experimental seminar exploring the human and cultural roots of modern mathematics.
motivation: The authors aim to study the human and cultural dimensions of mathematics through an experimental seminar format.
method: The paper presents reflections and observations from conducting an experimental seminar on the cultural and human roots of modern mathematics.
result: It offers qualitative insights and reflections rather than technical mathematical or scientific results.
conclusion: The work is a humanities-oriented reflection on mathematical practice, not a technical contribution to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Riemannian Density-Driven Optimal Control: Tangent-Space Lqr For Second-Order Multi-Agent Systems On Curved Manifolds
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) provides an effective framework for steering multi-agent systems toward prescribed spatial distributions. However, existing D2OC formulations are primarily developed for Euclidean domains and do not directly account for intrinsic manifold geometry. This paper extends D2OC to second-order multi-agent systems evolving on Riemannian manifolds. The proposed Riemannian D2OC (R-D2OC) constructs a local distribution objective in the tangent space of each agent through logarithmic maps and uses its weighted center as the reference for a finite-horizon LQR. The resulting control is executed on the manifold through intrinsic second-order dynamics and parallel transport within a receding-horizon scheme. We establish local curvature-dependent bounds that quantify the approximation introduced by the tangent-space reduction and characterize the resulting target bias. Furthermore, we derive a conditional discrete-descent result showing that the closed-loop objective decreases when a local velocity-alignment condition is satisfied. Numerical simulations on a 3D ellipsoidal manifold demonstrate distribution-level control and empirically support the proposed approximation and descent results.
tldr: The paper extends density-driven optimal control to second-order multi-agent systems on Riemannian manifolds using tangent-space LQR and parallel transport.
motivation: Existing density-driven optimal control formulations are mainly developed for Euclidean domains and ignore the intrinsic geometry of curved manifolds.
method: Riemannian D2OC constructs a local distribution objective in each agent's tangent space via logarithmic maps, takes its weighted center as the reference for finite-horizon LQR, and executes control on the manifold through intrinsic second-order dynamics and parallel transport in a receding-horizon scheme.
result: The authors derive local curvature-dependent bounds quantifying the tangent-space approximation error and target bias, and prove a conditional discrete-descent result for the closed-loop objective; simulations on a 3D ellipsoid demonstrate distribution-level control.
conclusion: The proposed framework enables density-driven control of multi-agent systems on curved manifolds, providing theoretical guarantees and numerical evidence.

title: Algorithmic Collusion And The Complexity Of Information-Value-Free Equilibria
abstract: ArXiv:2609.22757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A (coarse) correlated equilibrium (CE) is information-value-free (IVF) if a player can match the payoff obtained from recommendations by committing to a fixed action. Motivated by the problem of regulating algorithmic collusion, this refinement was introduced by Hartline, Wang, and Zhang [EC'26], who showed that it can be computed in polynomial time in explicitly represented normal-form game. In this paper, we examine the complexity of IVF(C)CEs in succinct games, which model more realistic strategic interactions that feature either many players or exponentially many pure strategies. We first show that computing an information-value-free CE is PPAD-complete in many-player polymatrix games or two-player Bayesian games, even when the approximation is a constant. We also prove an unconditional exponential query lower bound. Our results establish that IVFCEs are intractable, even in the centralized model, and rule out the existence of any efficient learning dynamics. This significantly strengthens the impossibility result of Hartline, Wang, and Zhang, which concerns a particular class of learning algorithms, and furnishes strong computational critiques of recent regulation on algorithmic collusion. To sidestep these hardness results, we examine the complexity of information-value-free CCE. Certain no-regret algorithms---such as regret matching or FTRL---provide a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for this problem. The complexity when the approximation is exponentially small turns out to be nuanced. On the one hand, leveraging no-regret dynamics, we establish membership in [MATH]. On the other hand, we show that it is at least as hard as the P-matrix linear complementarity problem, and hence as hard as simple stochastic games. This shows that even IVFCCEs are unlikely to admit a polynomial-time algorithm barring a major breakthrough.
tldr: Analysis failed

title: Exploiting Software-level Abstractions To Support Practical Hardware Trojan Attacks
authors: Athanasios Moschos, Kevin Valakuzhy, Georgios Kokolakis, Fabian Monrose, Angelos D. Keromytis
abstract: ArXiv:2609.23173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware trojan (HT) attacks against CPUs typically assume threat scenarios where an attacker targeting a system with a trojanized CPU is able to execute arbitrary code (i.e. machine-level instructions) to reliably interact with the implanted trojan. On end-user devices (i.e., mobiles, laptops), achieving arbitrary code execution in practice requires software exploits tailored to each specific target. Such strong adversarial premises reduce the generality of existing threat models casting doubt on CPU trojan attacks as a pragmatic threat vector. To push the envelope on HT attacks against client devices, we introduce the SURF class of CPU-trojans that can be activated without arbitrary code execution. Our key insight is that integer operations expressed in a high-level language can be mapped to microarchitectural side-effects distinguishable by a SURF trigger circuit. This observation unlocks HT activation via runtime engines, constrained environments executing untrusted high-level code. We demonstrate a SURF trojan inside a RISC-V processor and exploit JavaScript-level memory indexing operations inside Google's V8 engine to perform a code injection attack. Importantly, we show that SURF trojans remain effective across multiple JavaScript engine versions, enabling long-term compromise of endpoint devices. To facilitate research, we opensource SURF's design and supporting software.
tldr: Introduces SURF, a class of CPU hardware trojans that are activated via microarchitectural side effects of high-level language operations without requiring arbitrary code execution.
motivation: Existing hardware trojan threat models often assume arbitrary code execution, which is impractical on end-user devices; this work aims to show that practical trojan activation is possible through runtime engines executing untrusted high-level code.
method: The authors design a SURF trigger circuit inside a RISC-V processor that detects distinguishable microarchitectural side effects from integer operations, and demonstrate activation using JavaScript-level memory indexing operations in Google's V8 engine.
result: A SURF trojan successfully performs a code injection attack and remains effective across multiple JavaScript engine versions, enabling long-term compromise.
conclusion: Software-level abstractions can serve as a practical vector for hardware trojan attacks, and the open-sourced SURF design supports further research in this area.
